digSites.name: Crater of Diamonds State Park
digSites.summary: The only diamond-producing site in the world open to the public where you keep everything you find. A 37-acre plowed field sits atop an ancient volcanic pipe.
digSites.feeInfo: Adults $15, children (6–12) $7. Equipment rental available on site.
digSites.tips: Search after heavy rain — runoff washes soil away and exposes diamonds on the surface. Wet-sifting near the wash pavilion is the most productive method.

digSites.name: Wegner Quartz Crystal Mines
digSites.summary: Family-run quartz mines in the heart of Arkansas crystal country. Multiple dig experiences from surface scratching to deep mine access.
digSites.feeInfo: Crystal Forest dig $20/adult; Phantom mine tour from $75. Buckets sold separately.
digSites.tips: Bring gloves and a spray bottle — rinsing clusters in the field reveals the clearest points. Mount Ida is the self-proclaimed Quartz Crystal Capital of the World.

digSites.name: Emerald Hollow Mine
digSites.summary: The only emerald mine in the U.S. open to the public for prospecting. Sluice, creek, and dig your own across 70+ varieties of minerals.
digSites.feeInfo: Sluicing from $12; creeking $20; digging $20. All-access combo available.
digSites.tips: Creeking after rain is the best way to spot loose emerald crystals washed from the hillside. Staff can identify your finds for free.

digSites.name: Cherokee Ruby & Sapphire Mine
digSites.summary: Native, unenriched gravel means every ruby and sapphire you sluice was actually found at this Cowee Valley mine.
digSites.feeInfo: $25 per person per day, all the gravel you can dig and wash.
digSites.tips: Native dirt only — no salted buckets here, so finds are genuine. Wash gravel slowly and watch for the deep-red glint of ruby against the screen.

digSites.name: Graves Mountain
digSites.summary: A legendary collecting site famous for brilliant blue kyanite, lazulite, and rutile, open only during scheduled dig events each year.
digSites.feeInfo: Free during posted 'Rock Swap & Dig' weekends; donations welcome.
digSites.hours: Open only on scheduled event dates (spring & fall)
digSites.tips: Check the Georgia Mineral Society calendar before driving out — access is restricted to a few weekends per year. Bring sturdy boots for the loose tailings.

digSites.name: Hog Creek Public Dig Site
digSites.summary: Public Ouachita National Forest access for crystal digging. Fine clear quartz points and occasional amethyst clusters.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — National Forest land. Hand tools only.
digSites.tips: Hike in from the fire road — the best pockets are on the upper slopes. A pry bar and safety glasses are essential.

digSites.name: Crystal Grove Diamond Mine
digSites.summary: Family-friendly Herkimer diamond mining among the scenic Adirondack foothills, with easy surface collecting and deep pocket digging.
digSites.feeInfo: Adults $12, children $10. Hammer and chisel rental available.
digSites.tips: Look for the gray dolostone walls — Herkimers nest inside small cavities. Crack open with a light hammer and watch your fingers.

digSites.name: Morefield Mine
digSites.summary: A historic underground mine producing amazonite, topaz, and over 80 other mineral species from a complex pegmatite.
digSites.feeInfo: Adults $25, children $15. Dig from the mine dumps and underground adit.
digSites.tips: The underground adit is cool year-round — bring a jacket even in summer. Amazonite here is a striking blue-green feldspar.

digSites.name: Jackson's Crossroads Amethyst Mine
digSites.summary: World-class amethyst with deep purple saturation on white matrix, collected from an open-pit setting by appointment.
digSites.feeInfo: By appointment only; rates vary by dig type ($50–150).
digSites.tips: Reservations fill months in advance. The purple here rivals any amethyst in the world — bring plenty of newspaper for wrapping.

digSites.name: Diamond Hill Mine
digSites.summary: A prolific quartz and amethyst locality in the South Carolina piedmont with abundant skeletal and scepter quartz.
digSites.feeInfo: $20 per person per day. Buckets and tools available.
digSites.tips: Dig in the red clay pockets — that's where the finest skeletal and scepter crystals hide. Surface collecting is also productive after rain.

digSites.name: Hogg Mine
digSites.summary: Dig for rose quartz, black tourmaline, aquamarine, and beryl in a productive Georgia pegmatite mine.
digSites.feeInfo: $35 per person per day. Kids under 12 free with paying adult.
digSites.hours: Monthly dig days — check schedule online
digSites.tips: Following heavy rain, brilliant rose quartz chunks erode out of the pegmatite. Bring a shovel and sturdy bucket.

digSites.name: Franklin Gem & Mineral Museum
digSites.summary: Part of the historic Franklin mining district, with sluicing and digging across multiple mines nearby. Famous for sapphires and rubies.
digSites.feeInfo: Sluicing buckets from $10; guided digs from $30.
digSites.tips: The Franklin area has dozens of mines — the chamber of commerce can recommend which one is producing best this season.

digSites.name: Keenan Feldspar Quarry
digSites.summary: A classic Maine pegmatite quarry yielding aquamarine, morganite, garnet, and elbaite tourmaline from the famous Oxford County pegmatite belt.
digSites.feeInfo: Group digs arranged by local mineral clubs; inquire directly.
digSites.tips: Only accessible through organized club trips. The tourmalines here can be world-class gemmy crystals.

digSites.name: Herkimer Diamond Mines
digSites.summary: Hunt for doubly-terminated 'Herkimer diamonds' — exceptionally clear quartz crystals with 18 natural facets locked inside dolostone.
digSites.feeInfo: Adults $16, children $14. Hammers and hard hats available to rent.
digSites.tips: Crack open the hard grey dolostone pockets with a heavy hammer and chisel — the best crystals hide in vugs (cavities). Eye protection is required.

digSites.name: Sterling Hill Mining Museum
digSites.summary: World-famous fluorescent mineral locality with over 90 fluorescent species. Visit the museum and collect on the mine dumps.
digSites.tips: Bring a UV light — the fluorescent display here is the best in the world. The dump pile yields bright green willemite and red calcite that glow brilliantly.

digSites.name: Franklin Mineral Museum
digSites.summary: The fluorescent mineral capital of the world. Collect on the famous Buckwheat Dump and see the world's largest fluorescent display.
digSites.tips: This is a UV light collector's paradise — bring both shortwave and longwave lights. The dump pile still produces world-class specimens after decades.

digSites.name: Ace of Diamonds Mine
digSites.summary: Another classic Herkimer County locality with productive dolostone pockets yielding water-clear doubly-terminated quartz.
digSites.feeInfo: $12 per person per day. Tool rental available.
digSites.tips: New pockets are exposed by the owners regularly — ask at the office which area was most recently worked.

digSites.name: Garnet Hill
digSites.summary: Public BLM land where you can collect dark-red almandine garnets directly from the surface of a volcanic rhyolite ridge.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — BLM public land. Hand collecting permitted.
digSites.tips: The garnets weather out of the rhyolite and collect in small crevices. Bring a small rock hammer and hand lens — many garnets are perfect dodecahedrons.

digSites.name: Mount Apatite Park
digSites.summary: A public city park built around an abandoned feldspar quarry containing aquamarine, tourmaline, garnet, and smoky quartz.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public park. No power tools allowed.
digSites.tips: The main dumps near the parking area are most productive. Look for green and pink crystals in the white feldspar and mica matrix.

digSites.name: Gilsum Mine
digSites.summary: A historic beryl and tourmaline locality in the New England pegmatite belt. Known for green elbaite and golden beryl crystals.
digSites.feeInfo: Club access; contact Capital Mineral Club for dig dates.
digSites.tips: Deep pockets require heavy tools. Join the Capital Mineral Club to get on the dig roster — access is otherwise restricted.

digSites.name: Ron Coleman Mining
digSites.summary: One of the largest quartz crystal mines in the world. Massive commercial digging operation open to the public with abundant clear crystals.
digSites.feeInfo: Adults $25, children $15. Dig in tailings or the mine wall.
digSites.tips: Go for the fresh mine wall if you can — tailings are easier but the wall yields bigger, less damaged points. Rent a power washer for cleaning.

digSites.name: Cave-in-Rock Fluorite District
digSites.summary: The most famous fluorite locality in the world, producing purple, yellow, and blue cubes from Mississippi Valley-type deposits for over a century.
digSites.feeInfo: Several active mines take collectors; contact individual operators. Fees $20–50.
digSites.hours: Varies by mine — usually weekends by appointment
digSites.tips: Contact the American Fluorite Museum for a list of currently-open mines. The Annabel Lee and Denton mines are collector favorites.

digSites.name: Keokuk Geode Beds
digSites.summary: Iowa's tri-state geode region — crack open these bowling-ball-sized concretions to reveal quartz, calcite, and sometimes rare minerals inside.
digSites.feeInfo: Several pay-to-dig farms $10–20 per person. Riverbank collecting is free below high-water mark.
digSites.tips: Look for round, bumpy rocks in creek beds and road cuts. A heavy crack hammer works better than a standard rock hammer for these tough geodes.

digSites.name: Petoskey Stone Beaches
digSites.summary: Hunt for Michigan's state stone — fossilized colonial coral with a distinctive honeycomb pattern — along the Lake Michigan shoreline.
digSites.feeInfo: Free on public beaches. State park entry fee may apply.
digSites.tips: Wade in ankle-deep water after a storm — wave action exposes fresh Petoskey stones. They look like plain gray rocks when dry; keep a spray bottle to wet-test.

digSites.name: Lake Superior Agate Beaches
digSites.summary: The North Shore of Lake Superior is the premier hunting ground for the state gem — banded Lake Superior agates with rich reds, oranges, and yellows.
digSites.feeInfo: Free on public beaches and state parks.
digSites.tips: Walk gravel beaches at sunrise with the sun behind you — agates glow with a translucent, waxy luster that dull rocks lack. After storms is best.

digSites.name: Rock & Elk Copper Mine
digSites.summary: Collect native copper and datolite from spoil piles of the historic Keweenaw Peninsula copper district.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public mine dumps accessible year-round.
digSites.tips: Bring a metal detector — native copper and silver ring up unmistakably. The best specimens still have visible crystal forms.

digSites.name: Nethers Farm Flint Ridge
digSites.summary: Collect the world-famous Flint Ridge flint — Ohio's state gemstone — with its kaleidoscopic colors from a productive hillside quarry.
digSites.feeInfo: $8 per person per day. Buckets provided.
digSites.tips: Flint Ridge flint comes in every color — red, blue, pink, yellow, green. The quarry wall is the most productive spot; a rock hammer cracks out fresh material.

digSites.name: Cahaba River Fossil Beds
digSites.summary: Wade the Cahaba River to find fossils from the Cretaceous Western Interior Seaway — shark teeth, mosasaur bones, and ancient oysters.
digSites.feeInfo: Free on public access points. Some areas require Cahaba River NWR permit.
digSites.tips: Use a floating sifter or fine-mesh screen. The best fossil beds are in shallow riffles where gravel accumulates behind sandbars.

digSites.name: Isabella Pearl Mine
digSites.summary: Tennessee river-pearl collecting on a working freshwater mussel bed. Find natural baroque pearls in shades of pink, lavender, and gold.
digSites.feeInfo: $20 per person; keep what you find.
digSites.tips: Wear old clothes — you'll be wading chest-deep in the river with a viewing bucket. Most pearls are small but beautiful baroque shapes.

digSites.name: Crystal Mountain Fluorescent Mine
digSites.summary: Kentucky fluorite and fluorescent minerals from the Illinois-Kentucky fluorspar district, with UV collecting after dark.
digSites.hours: Sat 9:00 AM – 9:00 PM (night UV collecting offered)
digSites.tips: Stay for the night dig if you can — UV collecting here is extraordinary. The fluorites glow an intense blue-white under shortwave.

digSites.name: Llano Uplift Topaz Field
digSites.summary: Private ranch pay-to-dig for the famous light-blue Texas topaz — the state gem — from decomposed granite in the Llano Uplift.
digSites.feeInfo: Varies by ranch; typically $25–50 per person per day.
digSites.tips: The Lindsey and Seaquist ranches are the most well-known. Topaz here can be faceted into brilliant gems. A fine-mesh screen and hand trowel are your best tools.

digSites.name: Terlingua Calcite & Agate Fields
digSites.summary: Legendary West Texas collecting for fluorescent calcite, agates, and jaspers in the rugged Big Bend country.
digSites.feeInfo: Free on public BLM land. Some private ranches charge $10–20.
digSites.tips: Bring copious water — this is remote desert. The fluorescent calcite here glows brilliant pink-orange under UV. Collect after sunset with UV lights for best results.

digSites.name: Enchantment Agate Beds
digSites.summary: Remote BLM collecting for colorful moss agates, plume agates, and jaspers in the Chiricahua Mountain foothills.
digSites.tips: Walk the desert washes after summer monsoons — fresh agates get uncovered with each rain. A UV light at night helps some agates fluoresce.

digSites.name: Topaz Mountain
digSites.summary: Public BLM land where you can collect sherry-colored topaz, red beryl, and garnet from rhyolite. Free and open year-round.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public BLM land. No fees for hand collecting.
digSites.tips: Look in the cavities of the white-to-pink rhyolite. Amber topaz fades to clear in sunlight, so wrap finds to preserve color. Bring plenty of water — it's remote desert.

digSites.name: Oregon Sunstone Public Collection Area
digSites.summary: BLM-managed public area where you can dig for Oregon's official state gem — copper-bearing feldspar with a glittering schiller effect.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — BLM public land. Nearby private mines charge $50–100.
digSites.tips: The public area is free but heavily picked over — the private mines just outside the boundary yield richer stones. Bring a screen for dry-sifting.

digSites.name: Hallelujah Junction Petrified Wood
digSites.summary: Nevada/California border BLM area with rich deposits of colorful petrified and opalized wood near the site of a Pleistocene forest.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public BLM land. 25 lbs + 1 piece per day limit.
digSites.tips: Look for dark, heavy chunks with wood grain — some pieces are partially opalized with vivid colors. A rock saw reveals the inner beauty.

digSites.name: Royal Peacock Opal Mine
digSites.summary: Dig your own precious fire opal at one of America's few productive opal mines in the Virgin Valley of northern Nevada.
digSites.tips: Virgin Valley opals need to be kept in water — they can craze (crack) if dried too fast. Bring sealed containers.

digSites.name: Rainbow Ridge Opal Mine
digSites.summary: Another productive Virgin Valley opal mine with breathtaking play-of-color in blacks, reds, and greens.
digSites.tips: The black opal from Virgin Valley rivals Australian material. Work slowly in the bank walls — one good pocket can pay for the whole trip.

digSites.name: Diamond Peak Oregon
digSites.summary: High-elevation collecting for clear and smoky quartz crystals, occasional amethyst, and zeolites in the Cascade Range.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — National Forest land. Hand tools only.
digSites.tips: High-clearance vehicle required. The best crystals are in alpine pockets above 7,000 feet. Go in late summer after snowmelt.

digSites.name: Spencer Opal Mine
digSites.summary: Collect precious opal from a volcanic-hosted deposit in eastern Idaho. Known for triplets and jelly opals with translucent quality.
digSites.feeInfo: $25 per person per day. Keep what you find.
digSites.tips: The opal here forms thin layers in rhyolite — look for glassy, translucent patches on freshly broken rock surfaces.

digSites.name: Dugway Geode Beds
digSites.summary: Vast BLM collecting area famous for Dugway geodes with clear quartz and occasional amethyst-lined interiors.
digSites.tips: Geodes weather out of the rhyolite on the surface — walk slowly and scan for round rocks. The sound of a hollow rock when tapped is your best indicator.

digSites.name: Anderson Field Stone Quarry
digSites.summary: A sculptural field-stone quarry producing colorful flagstone, with mineral specimens including chrysocolla and azurite in the overburden.
digSites.tips: This is a working quarry — reach out to local mineral clubs for access. The copper secondaries here are among the best in Arizona.

digSites.name: Jade Cove
digSites.summary: A rugged stretch of Big Sur coastline famous for nephrite jade washing up among the cobbles below the cliffs.
digSites.feeInfo: Free public access. Collecting allowed below the mean high-tide line only.
digSites.tips: Hunt at low tide and look for waxy green stones that stay glossy when wet. The trail down is steep — wear grippy shoes. Never collect above the tide line.

digSites.name: Tourmaline Queen Mine
digSites.summary: The most famous tourmaline locality in North America — the Pala Chief and Tourmaline Queen mines produced world-record pink and green elbaite.
digSites.feeInfo: Fee digs available by reservation; $75–150 depending on area.
digSites.tips: The Oceanview Mine next door is the most active for public digs. Pala tourmalines are gem-quality — keep an eye out for watermelon (pink-and-green) crystals.

digSites.name: Oceanview Mine
digSites.summary: Active gem mine next door to the legendary Tourmaline Queen. Public fee digs for kunzite, tourmaline, and morganite.
digSites.tips: Screening through the mine tailings yields the most gems. Kunzite fades in sunlight — wrap your finds in aluminum foil immediately.

digSites.name: Himalaya Mine
digSites.summary: A storied San Diego County tourmaline mine that has produced some of the finest rubellite in the world since the 1890s.
digSites.feeInfo: Group digs by reservation; typically $100 per person.
digSites.tips: The pink tourmaline here is legendary — reddish-pink crystals on white albite matrix. Digs sell out fast so book early.

digSites.name: Stewart Mine
digSites.summary: A classic Pala district gem mine producing pink tourmaline, morganite, and kunzite from its famous lithium-rich pegmatite.
digSites.tips: This mine is less frequented than Oceanview — the tailings can be very productive. Look for bright pink rubellite fragments in the screened gravel.

digSites.name: Horse Canyon Agate Beds
digSites.summary: Desert collecting for moss agate, plume agate, and colorful jaspers in the southern Sierra Nevada foothills.
digSites.tips: Go in spring or fall — summer is dangerously hot. Walk the washes and look for glassy, translucent chunks that catch the light differently than surrounding rock.

digSites.name: Clear Creek Jade Fields
digSites.summary: A serpentine-rich BLM area yielding significant nephrite jade boulders in Clear Creek. Requires a long hike or ATV access.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public BLM land. Hand collecting only.
digSites.tips: This is serious jade hunting — boulders can weigh hundreds of pounds. Bring an ATV or be prepared for a 10+ mile round-trip hike. A rock hammer tests hardness.

digSites.name: Glass Buttes Obsidian
digSites.summary: Vast obsidian fields on BLM land with every variety imaginable — mahogany, rainbow, gold sheen, silver sheen, and midnight lace.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public BLM land. No collecting limits.
digSites.tips: Bring a pickup truck — large boulders are free for the taking. Rainbow obsidian shows its colors best when freshly broken. Safety glasses are mandatory.

digSites.name: Denio Thunderegg Beds
digSites.summary: Remote northern Nevada BLM area yielding thundereggs — spherical rhyolite masses with agate and opal centers.
digSites.tips: Thundereggs weather out as round lumps on the desert floor. Crack them open with a heavy hammer — the inside is a surprise every time.

digSites.name: San Carlos Apache Reservation
digSites.summary: The world's largest source of gem-quality peridot (olivine). On reservation land — guided collecting available through tribal permits.
digSites.feeInfo: Tribal permit required; inquire at San Carlos Apache office. Guided trips from $75.
digSites.tips: You're on sovereign tribal land — respect all rules and get the proper permit. The peridot here is luminous green and can be faceted into world-class gems.

digSites.name: Sheep Creek Garnet Area
digSites.summary: An Idaho Panhandle National Forest area where dark-red almandine garnets weather out of metamorphic schist into the creek beds.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — National Forest land. Hand tools only.
digSites.tips: Pan the creek gravel like you're looking for gold — the heavy garnets settle in the same places. Some show a 4-ray star when polished.

digSites.name: Papakolea Green Sand Beach
digSites.region: Ka Lae, Big Island, Hawaii, USA
digSites.summary: One of only four green sand beaches in the world, composed almost entirely of olivine sand eroded from an ancient cinder cone.
digSites.feeInfo: Free public access. 2.5-mile hike each way or paid shuttle.
digSites.tips: Do NOT take sand — it's culturally and ecologically protected. Admire and photograph the glittering green grains. Bring water — there's zero shade on the hike.

digSites.name: Jade Mountain
digSites.summary: Remote Alaskan nephrite jade deposits in the Brooks Range — one of the world's richest jade provinces, accessible only by bush plane.
digSites.feeInfo: Extremely remote — guided expeditions $2,500+ from Kotzebue.
digSites.tips: This is an expedition, not a day trip. Bush plane access only. The jade boulders here are enormous and of superb quality — plan a multi-day trip with an outfitter.

digSites.name: V-Rock Shop
digSites.summary: A beloved Ohio rock shop carrying an extensive selection of minerals, crystals, fossils, lapidary rough, and jewelry-making supplies. A must-stop for Midwest collectors.
digSites.feeInfo: Free to browse. Prices vary by specimen.
digSites.hours: Tue–Sat 10:00 AM – 6:00 PM, Sun 12:00 PM – 4:00 PM, Closed Mon
digSites.tips: Great selection of Ohio flint and regional minerals. The staff are knowledgeable and happy to help identify your finds.

digSites.name: Carlson's Rock World
digSites.summary: A beloved Iowa rock shop in Goldfield offering a wide selection of minerals, crystals, fossils, lapidary rough, and geodes from the Midwest and beyond. A must-stop for collectors driving through central Iowa.
digSites.feeInfo: Free to browse. Prices vary by specimen.
digSites.tips: Great source for Keokuk geodes from the nearby Iowa/Missouri border region. Ask about local dig site recommendations — the staff know the best public collecting spots in Wright County.

digSites.name: Main Street Rocks
digSites.summary: A friendly Michigan rock shop with a strong collection of Lake Superior agates, Petoskey stones, and regional minerals from the Great Lakes area.
digSites.feeInfo: Free to browse. Prices vary by specimen.
digSites.hours: Tue–Fri 11:00 AM – 5:00 PM, Sat 10:00 AM – 3:00 PM, Closed Sun–Mon
digSites.tips: The best place in Michigan for Lake Superior agates. Ask about their field trip recommendations for local hunting spots.

digSites.name: The Miners Gallery
digSites.summary: Premium Franklin, NC rock shop carrying local sapphires, rubies, and garnets from the Cowee Valley mines, plus worldwide specimens.
digSites.feeInfo: Free to browse. Fine specimens priced individually.
digSites.hours: Mon–Sat 10:00 AM – 5:00 PM, Sun by appointment
digSites.tips: Ask to see the locally-mined rough — they cut and facet stones from the Franklin area mines. Great place to buy a souvenir of your dig trip.

digSites.name: Avant Mining & Crystal Gallery
digSites.summary: Massive Arkansas crystal showroom featuring world-class quartz clusters, points, and museum pieces from Mount Ida and Hot Springs mines.
digSites.feeInfo: Free to browse. Specimens from $5 to $50,000+.
digSites.tips: They also run their own quartz mine nearby — ask about combo shop-and-dig packages. The museum-quality specimens upstairs are breathtaking.

digSites.name: Denver Gem & Mineral Showroom
digSites.summary: Year-round retail extension of the world-famous Denver Gem & Mineral Show, with thousands of specimens, gems, and educational displays.
digSites.tips: The best place in Colorado for Sweet Home Mine rhodochrosite — the state's iconic red mineral. Visit during the September show for the full experience.

digSites.name: Tucson Mineral & Fossil Co-op
digSites.summary: A collective of Arizona's best mineral, fossil, and lapidary dealers — an extension of the world's largest gem show (Tucson, every Jan–Feb).
digSites.feeInfo: Free to browse. All price ranges.
digSites.hours: Daily 10:00 AM – 6:00 PM (Jan–Feb extended hours for gem show)
digSites.tips: If you can't make the February gem show, this co-op is your year-round Tucson fix. Amazing Arizona copper minerals and Bisbee turquoise.

digSites.name: Maggie Valley Rock Shop
digSites.summary: A charming Smoky Mountain rock shop with strong selections of North Carolina rubies, sapphires, and emeralds, plus worldwide minerals and fossils.
digSites.feeInfo: Free to browse. Wide price range.
digSites.tips: They stock beautiful North Carolina emerald and hiddenite specimens. Friendly staff will point you to nearby dig-your-own mines.

digSites.name: Keystone Gallery
digSites.summary: Historic Black Hills rock shop near Mount Rushmore with an excellent selection of South Dakota rose quartz, Fairburn agates, and Black Hills gold.
digSites.hours: Daily 8:00 AM – 8:00 PM (seasonal; call for winter hours)
digSites.tips: The Fairburn agates here are stunning — with intricate fortification banding in reds, oranges, and pinks unique to South Dakota. A great stop after visiting Mount Rushmore.

digSites.name: Smithsonian Gem & Mineral Hall
digSites.summary: Home of the Hope Diamond and one of the world's finest mineral collections. Not a shop per se, but the premier destination for any rockhound visiting the nation's capital.
digSites.feeInfo: Free admission to the National Museum of Natural History.
digSites.tips: The National Gem Collection is jaw-dropping — the Hope Diamond, Logan Sapphire, and thousands of specimens in the vault. A must-see for any rockhound.

digSites.name: Harvard Mineralogical Museum
digSites.summary: Harvard's world-renowned mineral collection with over 400,000 specimens including the finest US collection of New England pegmatite minerals.
digSites.tips: The New England pegmatite specimens here are unmatched — giant beryl, tourmaline, and garnet crystals from Maine and Connecticut.

digSites.name: La Brea Tar Pits Museum Store
digSites.summary: The gift shop at the world's most famous Ice Age fossil site, carrying authentic saber-toothed cat and dire wolf fossil replicas, minerals, and scientific books.
digSites.feeInfo: Admission to museum: $15 adults. Shop is free to browse with admission.
digSites.tips: Best place in the country for authentic Ice Age fossil replicas and the real thing on display. Don't miss the active excavation pits outside.

digSites.name: Black Hills Institute Museum
digSites.summary: Home of 'Stan' the T. rex and an incredible fossil preparation lab. Their gift shop carries authentic dinosaur bone fragments, minerals, and educational materials.
digSites.feeInfo: Museum admission $12 adults. Shop free to browse.
digSites.hours: Mon–Sat 8:00 AM – 5:00 PM (Jun–Aug), reduced hours in winter
digSites.tips: This is where they cast the world's most famous T. rex skeletons. The gift shop sells authentic fossil bone fragments from the Hell Creek Formation — a genuine piece of dinosaur.

digSites.name: The Crystal Works
digSites.summary: A treasured Midwest rock shop in historic Galena specializing in geodes, Lake Superior agates, fluorite from southern Illinois, and worldwide crystals.
digSites.tips: The Illinois fluorite specimens here are spectacular — purple, blue, and yellow cubes from the now-closed mines of Hardin County. Grab one while you can.

digSites.name: Dixie Crystal Mining Co.
digSites.summary: Family-owned crystal shop and mine near Hot Springs with a huge selection of Arkansas quartz points, clusters, and wavellite from local mines.
digSites.feeInfo: Free to browse. Dig-your-own crystal mining available $25/person.
digSites.hours: Daily 8:00 AM – 5:00 PM (Mar–Nov), reduced winter hours
digSites.tips: They own their own crystal mine and the shop specimens are straight from the ground. Ask about the famous 'Wavellite' — a rare green Arkansas phosphate found nowhere else.

digSites.name: New Mexico Rock & Gem
digSites.summary: New Mexico's premier rock shop carrying local treasures — smithsonite from the Kelly Mine, fire agate, peridot, Apache tears, and Mexican minerals.
digSites.tips: The Kelly Mine smithsonite here is world-famous — robin's-egg blue and bubble-like botryoidal forms. Also great for Mexican wulfenite and fire agate.

digSites.name: Florida Rock Shack
digSites.summary: The go-to shop for Florida fossil hunters — megalodon teeth, mammoth fossils, fossilized coral, and agatized coral from the Peace River Formation.
digSites.tips: Best place in Florida for authentic megalodon teeth — from 1-inch to 6-inch monsters. Ask about Peace River fossil hunting trips.

digSites.name: Ed's House of Gems
digSites.summary: A Portland institution since 1952, carrying Oregon sunstone, thundereggs, petrified wood, picture jasper, and Pacific Northwest minerals.
digSites.tips: Oregon sunstone (feldspar with copper inclusions) is unique to Oregon — they have the best selection. Thundereggs (Oregon's state rock) are a must-buy.

digSites.name: California Rock & Mineral
digSites.summary: Located in the heart of the famous San Diego pegmatite district. Specializes in tourmaline (especially pink and watermelon), kunzite, morganite, and benitoite.
digSites.feeInfo: Free to browse. Fine specimens priced individually.
digSites.tips: San Diego County produces the world's finest pink tourmaline — ask to see the watermelon tourmaline slices. Benitoite (California's state gem) is also available.

digSites.name: Iroquois Coppermine
digSites.summary: A legendary Keweenaw Peninsula rock shop carrying native copper, datolite, prehnite, and Lake Superior agates. A must-visit for Michigan copper country collectors.
digSites.feeInfo: Free to browse. Copper specimens priced by weight and quality.
digSites.hours: Mon-Sat 10:00 AM - 6:00 PM, Sun 12:00 PM - 4:00 PM (Jun-Oct); call for off-season hours
digSites.tips: The Keweenaw produces the world's finest native copper crystals. Ask about nearby mine tailings for your own hunting.

digSites.name: Main Street Rocks
digSites.summary: The second location of this beloved Michigan rock shop, with Petoskey stones, Lake Superior agates, and fossils from the Great Lakes region.
digSites.feeInfo: Free to browse. Prices vary by specimen.
digSites.hours: Tue-Fri 11:00 AM - 6:00 PM, Sat 10:00 AM - 4:00 PM, Closed Sun-Mon
digSites.tips: Great Detroit-area spot for Petoskey and Charlevoix stones. They carry polished cabs and raw specimens for collectors at any level.

digSites.name: Burro Creek Agate & Collecting Area
digSites.summary: Desert creek bed on BLM land producing pastel-colored agate nodules, jasper, and occasional fire agate from volcanic deposits.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public BLM land. Walk-in access from Highway 93.
digSites.tips: The agate nodules are distinctive with their pastel purple, pink, and green hues. Go November–March to avoid the brutal summer heat.

digSites.name: Crabtree Emerald Mine
digSites.summary: The most famous emerald locality in the United States. Although the mine is no longer commercially worked, the adjacent Little Switzerland area hosts active mineral clubs.
digSites.feeInfo: Closed to individual collecting. Contact MAGMA club for group access.
digSites.tips: Access is through the Mountain Area Gem & Mineral Association (MAGMA). Join the club to get on the dig list for this legendary locality.

digSites.name: Ellenville Lead Mine
digSites.summary: Abandoned lead-zinc mine with galena, sphalerite, and rare secondary minerals in the Shawangunk Mountains.
digSites.feeInfo: Club access only. Contact Orange County Mineral Society.
digSites.tips: Dangerous old mine — never enter underground workings. The dumps outside produce bright galena cubes and fluorescent specimens.

digSites.name: Williams Quarry
digSites.summary: A classic Connecticut pegmatite quarry in the Middletown district known for beryl, columbite, and rare uranium minerals.
digSites.feeInfo: Club access. Contact Lapidary & Mineral Club of CT.
digSites.tips: Radioactive minerals abound — bring a Geiger counter if you have one. This is a serious collector locality best visited with an experienced club.

digSites.name: Pulsifer Quarry
digSites.summary: One of the most famous Maine pegmatite localities — type locality for the rare purple fluorapatite that glows under UV light.
digSites.feeInfo: Club access only. Contact Maine Mineralogical & Geological Society.
digSites.tips: The purple apatite here fluoresces a brilliant orange-pink. Extremely sought-after by collectors — these specimens command high prices.

digSites.name: Harrison Rutile Mine
digSites.summary: Near the famous Graves Mountain locality — additional rutile, kyanite, and pyrophyllite collecting in the same mineralized belt.
digSites.feeInfo: Open during Graves Mountain swap weekends (free).
digSites.hours: Same schedule as Graves Mountain events
digSites.tips: Visit on the same trip as Graves Mountain. The rutile here forms brilliant metallic-red needles. A hand lens reveals incredible crystal forms.

digSites.name: Sweet Home Mine (Collector Access)
digSites.summary: The world's most famous rhodochrosite locality — the Alma King and other museum specimens came from here. Very limited collector access.
digSites.feeInfo: Extremely limited. Collector access trips from $500+ when available.
digSites.tips: Sweet Home rhodochrosite is the Holy Grail for many collectors — deep cherry-red rhombic crystals. Join Collector's Edge mailing list for rare access opportunities.

digSites.name: Lake George Amazonite Locality
digSites.summary: World-class amazonite (blue-green microcline feldspar) with smoky quartz from the Pikes Peak pegmatite district.
digSites.feeInfo: Fee digs available through claim owners; typically $50–100 per day.
digSites.tips: The amazonite-smoky quartz combinations from Colorado are among the finest in the world. Claims near Crystal Peak and Harris Park are most productive.

digSites.name: Alma Rhodochrosite Tailings
digSites.summary: Mine dumps near the Sweet Home locality with small but collectible rhodochrosite, fluorite, and tetrahedrite specimens.
digSites.feeInfo: Some dumps are on public land (free); others require claim owner permission.
digSites.tips: These are the mine dumps from historical workings. You won't find museum pieces, but micro-mount and thumbnail specimens are plentiful with patience.

digSites.name: Helena Sapphire Gravels
digSites.summary: Sluice for Montana sapphires — pale blue, green, and occasional fancy colors — along the Missouri River gravel bars near Helena.
digSites.feeInfo: Public gravel bar access free. Nearby private mines charge $25–50.
digSites.tips: The sapphires are tiny but gemmy — a 10x loupe is essential. Screen the gravel just like gold panning; sapphires are heavier than surrounding rock.

digSites.name: Gem Mountain Sapphire Mine
digSites.summary: The most popular sapphire mine in Montana. Buy bags of gravel to wash on-site or take home — find rough sapphires and heat-treatable stones.
digSites.feeInfo: Gravel bags from $25; mine-run $80. Heat treatment available on-site.
digSites.tips: They'll heat-treat your finds to turn pale stones into vivid blues — a fascinating process to watch. The bigger the gravel bag, the better your odds.

digSites.name: Crystal Park Dig Area
digSites.summary: A National Forest fee dig area high in the Pioneer Mountains — dig for clear and smoky quartz, amethyst scepters, and occasional citrine.
digSites.tips: Elevation is over 9,000 feet — bring layers and watch for altitude sickness. The scepter amethysts here are distinctive with clear stems and purple tips.

digSites.name: Fire Agate Fields
digSites.summary: Remote Arizona desert locality for the elusive fire agate — a brown agate that reveals an internal play of fiery red, green, and gold when polished.
digSites.feeInfo: Free on BLM land. Some claims require permission.
digSites.hours: Daylight hours (Oct–Apr best, summer is dangerous)
digSites.tips: Fire agate looks like dull brown bubbly chalcedony on the outside — the fire is hidden inside. Carve a test window to check before carting heavy rocks home.

digSites.name: Baker Ranch Thundereggs
digSites.summary: Pay-to-dig on a private ranch for New Mexico thundereggs — distinctive with red and yellow agate centers.
digSites.feeInfo: $15 per person. Keep all you find.
digSites.tips: Call ahead to confirm they're open. The ranch roads can be rough after rain — a high-clearance vehicle helps. Each thunderegg is a surprise inside.

digSites.name: Rockhound State Park
digSites.summary: New Mexico state park dedicated to rock collecting — find agates, jasper, and geodes in the Little Florida Mountains. Take up to 15 lbs home.
digSites.tips: The best collecting is on the hillside trails above the campground. Look for translucent agate nodules weathering out of the volcanic rock. Bring a rock hammer.

digSites.name: Trinity River Agate Bars
digSites.summary: The Trinity River yields beautiful pastel agates, jaspers, and occasional jade washed down from the Klamath Mountains into river gravel bars.
digSites.feeInfo: Free on public river access points.
digSites.tips: Summer is best when water levels are low. Walk the gravel bars in the riverbed — look for waxy, translucent stones among the dull cobbles.

digSites.name: Hampton Butte Petrified Wood
digSites.summary: Central Oregon BLM area yielding green moss-agatized petrified wood with striking patterns from an ancient conifer forest.
digSites.tips: Look for dark green and rust-colored chunks — when cut, the moss agate patterns are spectacular. A rock saw reveals the hidden beauty.

digSites.name: Grand Marais Yooperlite Beach
digSites.summary: The most famous Yooperlite hunting beach on Lake Superior — sodalite-rich syenite glows fiery orange under UV light along miles of dark shoreline.
digSites.feeInfo: Free on public beaches. State park entry fee may apply at nearby Muskallonge Lake.
digSites.hours: Night hunting with UV light recommended — daytime hunting also productive after storms.
digSites.tips: Bring a 365nm UV flashlight for the best glow. Walk the beach at night after a storm — freshly exposed Yooperlites light up like glowing embers among the dark cobbles. The best stretch is east of the harbor.

digSites.name: Whitefish Point Beach
digSites.summary: The sandy-gravel shoreline at Whitefish Point in the Upper Peninsula yields Yooperlites, agates, and the occasional fossil washed from ancient sea beds.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — Whitefish Point is public land. Shipwreck Museum parking fee ($13) optional.
digSites.hours: Daylight to dusk; night UV hunting allowed on beach.
digSites.tips: Walk the shoreline east of the lighthouse toward Vermilion Point. The combination of shipwreck history and Yooperlite hunting makes this a bucket-list destination. Spring after ice-out is prime hunting.

digSites.name: Muskallonge Lake State Park Beach
digSites.summary: A quiet stretch of Lake Superior beach between Grand Marais and Whitefish Point where Yooperlites wash up alongside banded agates and unakite.
digSites.feeInfo: Michigan state park recreation passport required ($13 annual / $7 daily).
digSites.tips: The beach is less crowded than Grand Marais. Camp overnight and hunt at sunset — the campsites are steps from the shore. Look for the telltale orange fluorescence in the wave-washed cobble line.

digSites.name: Munising Yooperlite Shore
digSites.summary: The Pictured Rocks shoreline near Munising has recently emerged as a productive Yooperlite hunting ground, with the added bonus of agates and jasper in the same cobble beds.
digSites.feeInfo: Free on public beaches. Pictured Rocks National Lakeshore entry is free.
digSites.hours: Daylight hours; night UV hunting permitted on beach.
digSites.tips: Try Sand Point Beach or Miners Beach for the best hunting. Combine with a Pictured Rocks boat tour during the day and UV hunting at night — the contrast of daylight cliffs and nighttime fluorescence makes for an unforgettable trip.

digSites.name: Presque Isle Park Beach
digSites.summary: The black-stone beach at Presque Isle Park in Marquette is a reliable urban-proximate Yooperlite spot — sodalite cobbles stand out brilliantly against the dark basalt shoreline.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — Presque Isle Park is a city park.
digSites.tips: Park at the Black Rocks and walk north along the cobble shoreline. This is the most accessible Yooperlite beach with nearby amenities in Marquette. Best after northwest winds.

digSites.name: Great Sand Bay Yooperlite Beach
digSites.summary: At the tip of the Keweenaw Peninsula, Great Sand Bay mixes Yooperlite hunting with native copper and datolite in the same stretch — a mineral collector's paradise.
digSites.hours: Daylight hours; night UV hunting allowed.
digSites.tips: Hunt at low tide with both a UV light (for Yooperlites) and a regular flashlight (for copper). The Keweenaw is the only place on Earth where you can find native copper and fluorescent sodalite on the same beach walk.

digSites.name: McLain State Park Beach
digSites.summary: A long sandy-gravel beach on the Keweenaw Peninsula's western shore — McLain's exposed shoreline catches Yooperlites transported by the prevailing currents down the peninsula.
digSites.feeInfo: Michigan state park recreation passport required ($13 annual / $7 daily).
digSites.tips: Camp at the park for multi-day hunting. Walk west toward the breakwater after northwest winds — the best stones accumulate there. The park also has agate-hunting programs in summer.

digSites.name: Brimley State Park Beach
digSites.summary: At the eastern edge of the Upper Peninsula where Whitefish Bay meets Lake Superior, Brimley's beaches wash ashore Yooperlites alongside pudding stones and banded agates.
digSites.feeInfo: Michigan state park recreation passport required ($13 annual / $7 daily).
digSites.tips: This is the closest Yooperlite beach to the Mackinac Bridge — a good first stop for visitors driving up from the Lower Peninsula. Hunt the shoreline west of the campground for best results.

digSites.name: American Federation of Mineralogical Societies
digSites.summary: The national umbrella organization for hundreds of local gem, mineral, lapidary, and paleontology clubs across the United States. The best starting point for finding a club near you.
digSites.feeInfo: Membership is through your local affiliated club — annual dues vary (typically $15–$40/year).
digSites.hours: N/A — federation; join a local member club
digSites.tips: Use the AFMS club finder to locate a regional club near you. Most clubs host monthly meetings, annual shows, and organized field trips to dig sites you can't access on your own.

digSites.name: Tucson Gem & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: One of the oldest and most influential mineral clubs in the US, organizer of the world-famous Tucson Gem & Mineral Show. Hosts monthly meetings, educational programs, and member field trips.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings (Sep–May); TGMS Show in February
digSites.tips: Members get early access and volunteer opportunities at the legendary February Tucson Gem & Mineral Show — the premier mineral event in the world.

digSites.name: Pueblo Gem & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Active Colorado club hosting monthly meetings, lapidary workshops, an annual gem & mineral show, and member field trips to Colorado localities for amazonite, smoky quartz, and topaz.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in March
digSites.tips: Great access to Colorado pegmatite digs through member-only field trips. Beginners welcome — the club has a strong mentorship culture and a lapidary shop.

digSites.name: Michigan Mineralogical Society
digSites.summary: Detroit-based club founded in 1936, one of the oldest mineral societies in the Midwest. Hosts monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Lake Superior agates, Petoskey stones, and Upper Peninsula copper minerals.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings (Sep–May); annual show in spring
digSites.tips: Excellent for Great Lakes rockhounds. The club organizes trips to the Keweenaw Peninsula and Lake Superior beaches — the best way to access private collecting areas.

digSites.name: St. Louis Mineral & Gem Society
digSites.summary: Active Missouri club hosting monthly meetings, lapidary and silversmithing workshops, an annual gem show, and field trips for Missouri geodes, Mozarkite, and Calcite crystals.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in fall
digSites.tips: Members get access to private geode digs in northern Missouri — Keokuk geodes with beautiful quartz, calcite, and pyrite interiors. Bring a sledgehammer and safety glasses.

digSites.name: North Texas Gem & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Dallas-area club hosting monthly meetings, an annual gem & mineral show, lapidary workshops, and field trips for Texas topaz, agates, and fossils.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in spring
digSites.tips: The club organizes spring trips to Mason County for Texas topaz — the state gem — found in granite pegmatites. Bring a small garden rake and screen.

digSites.name: Idaho Gem Club
digSites.summary: Boise-based club founded in 1947, hosting monthly meetings, an annual gem & mineral show, and field trips for Idaho star garnet, jasper, agate, and petrified wood.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings (Sep–May); annual show in October
digSites.tips: Members get access to the Emerald Creek star garnet area and other Idaho localities. The star garnets from northern Idaho are found nowhere else in the US.

digSites.name: Pacific Northwest Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Pacific Northwest club hosting monthly meetings, lapidary workshops, an annual show, and field trips for Oregon sunstone, thundereggs, agate, and petrified wood.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in spring
digSites.tips: The best way to access private Oregon dig sites — sunstone mines in the high desert and thunderegg beds in central Oregon. The club has a fully-equipped lapidary shop for members.

digSites.name: Tampa Bay Mineral & Science Society
digSites.summary: Florida's most active mineral club, hosting monthly meetings, an annual gem & mineral show, and field trips for Florida fossils — megalodon teeth, agatized coral, and Peace River finds.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in November
digSites.tips: The club runs organized Peace River fossil hunting trips — the best way to find megalodon teeth and fossil mammal bones. They provide screens and training for first-timers.

digSites.name: Lake Superior Gem & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Upper Peninsula club dedicated to Lake Superior agate hunting, Yooperlite hunting, Keweenaw copper minerals, and the local geology of the Marquette Iron Range.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in summer
digSites.tips: The most knowledgeable group for Yooperlite hunting on Lake Superior beaches. Members know the exact beaches and conditions that produce the best fluorescent sodalite finds.

digSites.name: Sacramento Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Northern California club hosting monthly meetings, an annual gem & mineral show, lapidary workshops, and field trips for California gold, quartz crystals, and tourmaline.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in spring
digSites.tips: Members get access to gold-panning trips in the Mother Lode and quartz crystal digs in the Sierra Nevada. The club also runs a lapidary workshop with cabochon machines.

digSites.name: Cabarrus Gem & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Active North Carolina club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips to the Carolina slate belt for quartz, emerald, ruby, sapphire, and monazite.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in spring
digSites.tips: Great for access to the famous Hiddenite emerald digs and Cowee Valley ruby/sapphire gravels. The club organizes group trips to otherwise-fee mines at member rates.

digSites.name: Lincoln Gem & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Nebraska's primary mineral club, hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, lapidary workshops, and field trips for Fairbury agate, Blue chalcedony, and Ogallala formation fossils.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in spring
digSites.tips: The club runs field trips to the Blue River beds for Nebraska's distinctive blue chalcedony — found nowhere else. Beginners welcome with an active junior rockhounds program.

digSites.name: Seattle Mineral & Gem Society
digSites.summary: Pacific Northwest club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, a fully-equipped lapidary workshop, and field trips for Washington minerals — quartz, pyrite, fossils, and Ellensburg blue agate.
digSites.feeInfo: Annual membership ~$30 individual / $40 family. Lapidary shop access included.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; shop open weekly for members
digSites.tips: One of the best-equipped lapidary shops in the PNW — members can use cabochon machines, slab saws, and faceting equipment. The Ellensburg blue agate field trips are a highlight.

digSites.name: Mid-Hudson Valley Gem & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Hudson Valley club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for New York minerals — Herkimer diamonds, garnet, tourmaline, and Connecticut pegmatite minerals.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in spring
digSites.tips: The club organizes trips to Herkimer County for the famous doubly-terminated quartz 'diamonds' — the best access to private digs in the area.

digSites.name: Rocky Mountain Federation of Mineralogical Societies
digSites.summary: The regional federation covering 11 western states — connects rockhounds to dozens of affiliated local clubs across the Rockies and Great Plains. Sponsors an annual convention and rotating show.
digSites.feeInfo: Membership is through your local affiliated club.
digSites.hours: Annual convention rotates among member clubs
digSites.tips: If you're in a Rocky Mountain or Great Plains state, start here to find a local club. The annual convention features guided field trips to regional dig sites that are otherwise closed to the public.

digSites.name: Alabama Mineral & Lapidary Society
digSites.summary: Birmingham-area club hosting monthly meetings, an annual gem & mineral show, lapidary workshops, and field trips for Alabama hematite, quartz, and Bancroft talc.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in fall
digSites.tips: Alabama is the source of the state mineral, hematite (red iron ore). The club organizes trips to historic iron-ore districts and Quartz Crystal localities.

digSites.name: Anchorage Gem & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Alaska's largest mineral club, hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Alaska jade, gold, garnet, and quartz from the Last Frontier.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings (Sep–May); annual show in spring
digSites.tips: Alaska's state gem is nephrite jade, found in the Kobuk River area. Members organize summer trips to jade and gold localities accessible only by bush plane or boat.

digSites.name: Crater Rock & Gem Club
digSites.summary: Hot Springs-area club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, lapidary workshops, and field trips to Arkansas quartz crystal mines and the Crater of Diamonds.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in September
digSites.tips: Members get organized trips to the Crater of Diamonds State Park — the only public diamond dig in the US. Bring a sifter, a trowel, and patience.

digSites.name: Connecticut Valley Mineral Club
digSites.summary: Central Connecticut club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Connecticut garnet, beryl, tourmaline, and the famous Portland Quarry minerals.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in March
digSites.tips: Connecticut has the famous garnet dig at Roxbury and historic pegmatite quarries. The club arranges access to otherwise-closed localities.

digSites.name: Delaware Mineralogical Society
digSites.summary: Delaware's primary mineral club, hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Delaware/Pennsylvania quartz, garnet, and Cretaceous fossils.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in spring
digSites.tips: Delaware's state mineral is sillimanite, found in the Brandywine region. The club also hunts Cretaceous fossils at the C&D Canal — a unique Delaware locality.

digSites.name: Georgia Mineral Society
digSites.summary: One of the oldest and largest mineral societies in the Southeast, founded in 1935. Hosts monthly meetings, an annual show, lapidary workshops, and field trips for Georgia staurolite, quartz, and rutile.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings (Sep–May); annual show in October
digSites.tips: Georgia's state mineral is staurolite (fairy crosses) — found in Fannin and Gilmer Counties. The club runs trips to the famous Graves Mountain locality for rutile and lazulite.

digSites.name: Hawaii Rock & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Hawaii's mineral club focused on the islands' unique volcanic geology — olivine, peridot, basalt, and obsidian. Hosts monthly meetings and occasional inter-island field trips.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; periodic beach and volcanic field trips
digSites.tips: Papakolea (Green Sand Beach) on the Big Island is one of only four green-sand beaches in the world — the green is olivine. Members organize guided trips and identify volcanic finds.

digSites.name: Illinois Valley Gem & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Northern Illinois club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, lapidary workshops, and field trips for Illinois fluorite, geodes, and Mazon Creek fossils.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in summer
digSites.tips: Southern Illinois is the fluorite capital of the US — the famous Cave-in-Rock district. The state mineral is fluorite. Members organize trips to the Ben E. Clement Mineral Museum and historic mines.

digSites.name: Indiana Geology & Gem Society
digSites.summary: Central Indiana club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, lapidary workshops, and field trips for Indiana geodes, Salem limestone fossils, and glaciers-carried agates.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in November
digSites.tips: Indiana is famous for the Bloomington-Bedford limestone belt — the Salem Limestone carries beautiful fossil hash. The club also hunts geodes in the Harrodsburg area.

digSites.name: Iowa Gem & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Iowa's primary mineral club, hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Keokuk geodes, Iowa agates, and glacial erratic minerals.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in spring
digSites.tips: The Keokuk geode beds along the Mississippi are Iowa's signature find — beautiful quartz and calcite interiors. The state rock is the geode.

digSites.name: Kansas Geology & Gem Society
digSites.summary: South-central Kansas club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Kansas agates, Niobrara chalk fossils, and the famous Wallace County megafossils.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in March
digSites.tips: Western Kansas produces spectacular Cretaceous fossils in the Niobrara Chalk — including shark teeth and marine reptile bones. The state mineral is galena, found in the Tri-State district.

digSites.name: Blue Grass Gem & Mineral Club
digSites.summary: Central Kentucky club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Kentucky agates, geodes, fluorite, and the famous Kentucky fluorite district.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in fall
digSites.tips: Eastern Kentucky produces the state rock, the Kentucky Agate — banded red, yellow, and gray. The club also hunts the historic Illinois-Kentucky Fluorspar District.

digSites.name: Crescent City Gem & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Gulf Coast club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Louisiana petrified wood, agate, citrine, and gravel-bar minerals.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in spring
digSites.tips: Louisiana's state mineral is agate, carried south by ancient river gravels. The club organizes gravel-bar trips along the Tickfaw and Tangipahoa rivers for petrified wood and agate.

digSites.name: Maine Mineral & Gem Society
digSites.summary: Maine's premier mineral club, hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Maine tourmaline, beryl, aquamarine, and the famous New England pegmatites.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in July
digSites.tips: Maine is world-famous for tourmaline — the state mineral. The Havey and Mount Mica quarries produce world-class elbaite. The club arranges access to otherwise-private pegmatite digs.

digSites.name: Maryland Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Baltimore-area club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Maryland minerals — Patuxent River agate, Chrome spinel, and the famous State Line serpentine district.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in March
digSites.tips: The State Line serpentine district (MD/PA border) produces the state gem, chrome spinel. The club also hunts Miocene fossils at Calvert Cliffs — a famous shark-tooth locality.

digSites.name: Minnesota Mineral Club
digSites.summary: Twin Cities club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Lake Superior agate, Minnesota's state gemstone, plus Thomsonite, pipestone, and glacial erratics.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in November
digSites.tips: The Lake Superior agate is Minnesota's state gemstone — found in gravel pits and river gravels across the state, carried by glaciers. The club also organizes trips to Pipestone National Monument area.

digSites.name: Mississippi Gem & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Central Mississippi club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Mississippi agates, fossils, and the famous Catahoula banded agate.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in February
digSites.tips: The Catahoula banded agate, found in gravel deposits across central Mississippi, is one of the most beautiful American agates. The state stone is petrified wood.

digSites.name: Missoula Gem & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Western Montana club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, lapidary workshops, and field trips for Montana sapphire, agate, and quartz crystals.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in October
digSites.tips: Western Montana produces world-famous sapphires — Rock Creek, Dry Cottonwood Creek, and the famous Yogo Gulch. Members organize trips to public sapphire gravels.

digSites.name: Southern Nevada Gem & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Las Vegas-area club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Nevada turquoise, opal, azurite, and the famous Nevada opal district.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in November
digSites.tips: Nevada produces world-class turquoise (state mineral) from mines like Carico Lake and Royston. The Virgin Valley opal district produces precious black opal — the only US source.

digSites.name: Keene Mineral Club
digSites.summary: Southwestern New Hampshire club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for New Hampshire beryl, smoky quartz, fluorite, and the famous Palermo Mine minerals.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in August
digSites.tips: New Hampshire is famous for the Palermo Mine — one of the most species-diverse pegmatites in the world. The state mineral is beryl, and the state gem is smoky quartz.

digSites.name: New Jersey Mineralogical Society
digSites.summary: Northern New Jersey club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for New Jersey prehnite, zeolites, and the famous Watchung Traprock minerals.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in spring
digSites.tips: The Watchung Mountains traprock quarries produce world-class prehnite and zeolite specimens. The club arranges access to active quarries that are otherwise off-limits to collectors.

digSites.name: Albuquerque Gem & Mineral Club
digSites.summary: Central New Mexico club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, lapidary workshops, and field trips for New Mexico turquoise, beryl, quartz, and the famous Harding Mine minerals.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in March
digSites.tips: New Mexico's state gem is turquoise, mined for centuries at Cerrillos and the Burro Mountains. The Harding Mine produces world-class lepidolite and spodumene crystals.

digSites.name: Dakota Mineral & Gem Club
digSites.summary: Central North Dakota club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for North Dakota glacial erratics, petrified wood, and the famous Cannonball concretions.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in spring
digSites.tips: North Dakota's state fossil is the Teredo-bored petrified wood, found in the Badlands. The Theodore Roosevelt National Park area produces unique cannonball-shaped siderite concretions.

digSites.name: Akron Mineral & Gem Society
digSites.summary: Northeast Ohio club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, lapidary workshops, and field trips for Ohio flint, fluorite, and the famous Flint Ridge artifacts.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in October
digSites.tips: Ohio's state gemstone is flint, especially Flint Ridge flint — used by Native Americans for thousands of years. The club also hunts the famous Ohio River agates and fossils.

digSites.name: Tulsa Rock & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Northeastern Oklahoma club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Oklahoma selenite, barite roses, and the famous Great Salt Plains crystals.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in March
digSites.tips: Oklahoma's state crystal is selenite from the Great Salt Plains — the only place in the world where hourglass-shaped selenite crystals form. The state rock is the barite rose.

digSites.name: Philadelphia Mineralogical Society
digSites.summary: One of the oldest mineral societies in the US, founded in 1892. Hosts monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Pennsylvania quartz, pyrite, and the famous Cornish pegmatites.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings (Sep–May); annual show in March
digSites.tips: Pennsylvania has historic mineral localities including the famous Cornwall iron mines and the French Creek pyrite locality. Members get access to working quarries in the Delaware Valley.

digSites.name: Rhode Island Mineral Hunters
digSites.summary: Rhode Island's mineral club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Rhode Island bowenite, beryl, and Connecticut Valley pegmatite minerals.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in October
digSites.tips: Rhode Island's state mineral is bowenite — a variety of serpentine found in the Conimicut area. The club also hunts the nearby Connecticut pegmatite quarries for beryl and garnet.

digSites.name: Western South Carolina Gem & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Upstate South Carolina club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for South Carolina amethyst, smoky quartz, and Blue Ridge minerals.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in spring
digSites.tips: South Carolina's state gem is amethyst, found in the Diamond Hill mine area. The club organizes trips to the Reedy River and Blue Ridge localities for smoky quartz and garnet.

digSites.name: Black Hills Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Western South Dakota club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Black Hills minerals — rose quartz, beryl, feldspar, and the famous Scotts Rose Quartz mine.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in July
digSites.tips: South Dakota's state mineral is rose quartz, mined in the Black Hills — the Scotts Rose Quartz mine is the world's largest. The Hills also produce feldspar, mica, and beryl.

digSites.name: Middle Tennessee Rockhounds
digSites.summary: Central Tennessee club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Tennessee agate, geodes, calcite, and the famous Tennessee painted agate.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in fall
digSites.tips: Tennessee is famous for the rare Tennessee Painted Agate, found in the central part of the state. The club also hunts the Elmwood Mine fluorite and sphalerite district.

digSites.name: Rocky Mountain Gem & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Wasatch Front club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, lapidary workshops, and field trips for Utah topaz, red beryl, variscite, and the famous Dugway geodes.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in October
digSites.tips: Utah's state gem is topaz (from Topaz Mountain), and the state mineral is copper. Utah is the only source of red beryl (the rarest beryl in the world) from the Wah Wah Mountains.

digSites.name: Vermont Mineral & Gem Club
digSites.summary: Northern Vermont club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Vermont garnet, talc, asbestos, and the famous Roxbury garnet locality.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in summer
digSites.tips: Vermont's state mineral is grossular garnet, found in the famous Belvidere Mountain asbestos/talc complex. The club organizes trips to the Roxbury garnet locality and Adamant pegmatite.

digSites.name: Northern Virginia Mineral Club
digSites.summary: Northern Virginia club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Virginia amazonite, staurolite, quartz, and the famous Rappahannock river agates.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in spring
digSites.tips: Virginia's state mineral is a dark blue amazonite (variety of microcline feldspar) found in the Morefield Mine. The state rock is unakite, found in the Blue Ridge.

digSites.name: Kanawha Rock & Mineral Club
digSites.summary: Central West Virginia club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for West Virginia fossils, quartz, and the famous Hillsboro siderite concretions.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in October
digSites.tips: West Virginia's state gem is the silicified Mississippian fossil coral Lithostrotion, found in the Greenbrier Limestone. The state rock is bituminous coal — fossil fuel history.

digSites.name: Kettle Moraine Gem & Mineral Society
digSites.summary: Southeastern Wisconsin club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Lake Superior agates, Wisconsin fossils, and glacial drift minerals.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in May
digSites.tips: Wisconsin's state mineral is galena, mined historically in the southwest corner (the lead rush of the 1820s). The state rock is red granite — found in glacial erratics across the state.

digSites.name: Natrona County Rock & Gem Club
digSites.summary: Central Wyoming club hosting monthly meetings, an annual show, and field trips for Wyoming jade, agate, fossils, and the famous Wyoming nephrite jade localities.
digSites.hours: Monthly meetings; annual show in summer
digSites.tips: Wyoming's state gem is nephrite jade — found in the Granite Mountains and Jeffrey City area. The club organizes trips to jade localities and the famous Titanotheres fossil beds.

digSites.name: The Crystal Vortex
digSites.summary: A Sedona vortex-area metaphysical shop specializing in healing crystals, aura quartz, selenite towers, and energetically charged specimens from around the world.
digSites.feeInfo: Free to browse. Crystals priced individually.
digSites.tips: Sedona's energy vortexes draw crystal enthusiasts from around the world. Ask about locally sourced Arizona quartz and citrine clusters.

digSites.name: House of Intuition
digSites.summary: A beloved LA metaphysical shop with an extensive crystal collection, tarot decks, singing bowls, and energy healing tools.
digSites.tips: Great selection of large selenite towers and spheres. Ask staff about crystal grids and energy work recommendations.

digSites.name: The Spellbound
digSites.summary: Santa Fe's premier metaphysical crystal shop featuring healing stones, Native American fetishes, and New Mexico minerals.
digSites.hours: Mon–Sat 10:00 AM – 6:00 PM, Sun 12:00 PM – 5:00 PM
digSites.tips: Ask about authentic New Mexico turquoise and staurolite (fairy cross) specimens from Taos County.

digSites.name: Earthly Treasures
digSites.summary: An eclectic Asheville metaphysical shop with a curated crystal collection, healing wands, and North Carolina local minerals.
digSites.tips: Asheville's crystal scene is booming. Ask about North Carolina ruby and sapphire crystals from the Cowee Valley.

digSites.name: Crystal Rising
digSites.summary: A vibrant Portland metaphysical shop with healing crystals, crystal grids, and an impressive selection of large display specimens.
digSites.tips: Best place in Portland for Oregon sunstone specimens. Their crystal grid kits are perfect for energy work beginners.

digSites.name: AzureGreen
digSites.summary: A long-standing NYC metaphysical supply shop with an extensive crystal and mineral section serving the East Coast community.
digSites.hours: Mon–Sat 11:00 AM – 8:00 PM, Sun 12:00 PM – 6:00 PM
digSites.tips: Ask about authentic Herkimer diamonds from upstate New York mines. Great selection of tumbled and raw healing stones.

digSites.name: Crystal Soul
digSites.summary: A Chicago metaphysical boutique with healing crystals, singing bowls, and mineral specimens from fluorite country.
digSites.tips: Illinois fluorite from Cave-in-Rock is featured here — ask to see the purple and yellow cubic specimens.

digSites.name: Spirit Crystals
digSites.summary: Austin's go-to metaphysical crystal shop with Texas topaz, healing wands, chakra stones, and a wide selection of spheres and towers.
digSites.tips: Ask about Texas topaz from the Llano Uplift — the state gem. Their selenite lamp collection is stunning.

digSites.name: The Crystal Garden Denver
digSites.summary: A Denver metaphysical store with healing crystals, Colorado rhodochrosite, amazonite, and an extensive smoky quartz collection.
digSites.hours: Mon–Sat 10:00 AM – 7:00 PM, Sun 12:00 PM – 5:00 PM
digSites.tips: Colorado rhodochrosite and Pikes Peak amazonite are the highlights. Ask about locally mined specimens.

digSites.name: Moon Body Soul
digSites.summary: A Pacific Northwest metaphysical shop with healing crystals, chakra sets, and Washington state minerals including zeolites and quartz.
digSites.tips: Ask about Washington zeolites from the Cascade Range — stilbite and heulandite are local favorites.

digSites.name: Mystic Dreams Crystal Shop
digSites.summary: A South Florida metaphysical boutique with Caribbean and South American crystals, healing tools, and an impressive geode collection.
digSites.hours: Mon–Sat 10:00 AM – 8:00 PM, Sun 12:00 PM – 6:00 PM
digSites.tips: Great selection of large Brazilian amethyst geodes and Uruguayan amethyst clusters. Ask about wholesale deals on clusters.

digSites.name: Temple of Crystals
digSites.summary: A Nashville metaphysical shop featuring Tennessee crystal pearls, healing wands, and a wide selection of tumbled and raw stones.
digSites.tips: Tennessee freshwater pearls are a unique local specialty. Ask about pearl hunting on the Tennessee River.

digSites.name: Aura Wellness & Crystals
digSites.summary: A Boston-area metaphysical shop with New England pegmatite minerals, healing crystals, and meditation tools.
digSites.hours: Mon–Sat 10:00 AM – 7:00 PM, Sun 12:00 PM – 5:00 PM
digSites.tips: New England pegmatite minerals are featured — Maine tourmaline and Connecticut beryl. Ask about local collecting sites.

digSites.name: Crystal Cove
digSites.summary: A Phoenix metaphysical shop with Arizona copper minerals, chrysocolla, malachite, and a full range of healing crystals.
digSites.tips: Arizona copper minerals are the highlight — ask about Bisbee malachite and Morenci chrysocolla specimens.

digSites.name: The Goddess Tree
digSites.summary: An Atlanta metaphysical boutique with Georgia minerals, healing crystals, crystal grids, and energy healing workshops.
digSites.hours: Tue–Sat 11:00 AM – 7:00 PM, Sun 12:00 PM – 5:00 PM, Closed Mon
digSites.tips: Georgia kyanite and Graves Mountain rutile are local specialties. Ask about upcoming crystal workshops.

digSites.name: Rocks & Gems Houston
digSites.summary: A Houston metaphysical and rock shop with healing crystals, Texas minerals, and an extensive geode and sphere collection.
digSites.hours: Mon–Sat 10:00 AM – 7:00 PM, Sun 12:00 PM – 5:00 PM
digSites.tips: Their amethyst geode cave collection rivals any in Texas. Ask about bulk tumbled stone deals.

digSites.name: Earth Born Market
digSites.summary: A Boulder metaphysical shop with Colorado minerals, healing crystals, and a focus on ethically sourced specimens.
digSites.tips: Colorado amazonite-smoky quartz assemblages from the Pikes Peak area are their signature. Ask about ethically sourced specimens.

digSites.name: Spiritual Journey
digSites.summary: A Philadelphia metaphysical shop with healing crystals, Pennsylvania minerals, and a strong selection of large display pieces.
digSites.tips: Ask about Pennsylvania pyrite specimens from the historic mining districts. Their large celestite geodes are spectacular.

digSites.name: Crystal Visions
digSites.summary: A Madison metaphysical shop with healing crystals, Midwest minerals, and a popular crystal grid and chakra set selection.
digSites.hours: Mon–Sat 10:00 AM – 6:00 PM, Sun 12:00 PM – 4:00 PM
digSites.tips: Wisconsin galena and fluorite specimens are local highlights. Ask about Midwest mineral collecting trips.

digSites.name: The Rock Shop
digSites.summary: A charming Savannah metaphysical shop with healing crystals, Georgia minerals, and an inspiring collection of tumbled and raw stones.
digSites.tips: Georgia kyanite blades are a unique local find. Their tumbled stone bins are great for budget-conscious collectors.

digSites.name: Four Winds Rock & Gift
digSites.summary: A Bar Harbor rock shop specializing in Maine pegmatite minerals — tourmaline, beryl, aquamarine, and morganite — plus worldwide specimens.
digSites.tips: Maine tourmaline from the Oxford County pegmatite belt is the highlight. Ask about local dig-your-own sites.

digSites.name: Treasure Mountain Mining
digSites.summary: A premier New England rock shop with worldwide mineral specimens, lapidary rough, and an extensive online catalog.
digSites.tips: One of the best mineral shops in New England. Their New England pegmatite collection is exceptional.

digSites.name: Mama's Minerals
digSites.summary: A large Albuquerque rock and metaphysical shop with New Mexico minerals, fossils, beads, and lapidary supplies.
digSites.hours: Mon–Sat 10:00 AM – 6:00 PM, Sun 12:00 PM – 5:00 PM
digSites.tips: Best place in Albuquerque for New Mexico turquoise and Kelly Mine smithsonite. They also carry beads and lapidary supplies.

digSites.name: Amethyst Mine Panorama Shop
digSites.summary: Canadian amethyst shop at the world's largest amethyst mine open to the public. Thunder Bay amethyst has distinctive red hematite inclusions.
digSites.feeInfo: Dig your own: $5 per pound. Shop free to browse.
digSites.tips: Thunder Bay amethyst is unique — the deep purple crystals have red hematite inclusions making them highly sought after by collectors.

digSites.name: Emerald Creek Garnet Area
digSites.summary: US Forest Service fee dig area for star garnets — Idaho's state gem. One of only two places in the world where star garnets are found.
digSites.tips: Screen the creek gravel like gold panning — the heavy garnets settle in the same spots. Star garnets show 4 or 6-ray stars when polished.

digSites.name: Fairburn Agate Beds
digSites.summary: The type locality for South Dakota's state gemstone — Fairburn agates with spectacular fortification banding in reds, pinks, and whites.
digSites.feeInfo: Free on BLM and National Grassland land.
digSites.tips: Walk the gullies and erosion channels after rain. Fairburn agates look like ugly brown rocks on the outside — crack them to reveal the beauty.

digSites.name: Painted Hills Agate Area
digSites.summary: Bureau of Land Management area near the Painted Hills with thundereggs, agates, and petrified wood in a stunning desert landscape.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — BLM land. 25 lb daily limit.
digSites.tips: The colorful hills are off-limits for collecting, but surrounding BLM land is open. Look for round thundereggs weathered out of volcanic ash beds.

digSites.name: Estherville Meteorite Site
digSites.summary: Site of the famous 1879 Estherville meteorite fall — a rare mesosiderite stony-iron meteorite. No active collecting, but historically significant.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — historical site. No active meteorite collecting.
digSites.tips: The Estherville fall scattered hundreds of pounds of meteorite fragments over a 10-mile area. Historical site only — metal detect surrounding farm fields with permission.

digSites.name: Streaked Canyon Jasper Field
digSites.summary: Remote Mojave Desert BLM area yielding colorful picture jasper, orbicular jasper, and agate nodules.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — BLM land. Hand collecting only.
digSites.tips: Go in winter or early spring. Walk the dry washes after rain — jasper nodules stand out with their waxy luster against the desert floor.

digSites.name: McKee Creek Fossil Area
digSites.summary: Central California BLM area with shark teeth, marine mammal fossils, and petrified wood from the Miocene-era Temblor Formation.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — BLM land. Casual collecting allowed.
digSites.tips: Screen the creek gravel for small shark teeth and ray dental plates. After winter rains, new material is exposed along the embankments.

digSites.name: Malpais Jasper Beds
digSites.summary: New Mexico BLM desert area with red and yellow jasper, agate nodules, and occasional peridot from the Rio Grande rift volcanic field.
digSites.tips: The red and yellow jasper here forms in distinctive bands. Look for float material in the arroyos after monsoon season.

digSites.name: Big Brook Fossil Creek
digSites.summary: A New Jersey creek famous for Cretaceous marine fossils — shark teeth, belemnites, and the occasional mosasaur tooth.
digSites.tips: Wade the creek with a sifting screen. The gravel bars contain shark teeth from the Navesink Formation. Best after heavy rain.

digSites.name: Cedar Creek Fossil Beds
digSites.summary: Idaho creek beds with Cambrian and Ordovician fossils — trilobites, brachiopods, and echinoderm fragments from ancient seafloor deposits.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public access along the creek.
digSites.tips: Split the grey shale layers with a rock hammer — trilobites are common in the slightly weathered beds. Bring a splitting chisel.
