digSites.name: Calico Mountains Agate Field
digSites.summary: Historic Mojave Desert collecting area for dendritic agate, jasper, and mineralized specimens from the Calico Mining District.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — BLM land. Some areas within the Calico Ghost Town fee area.
digSites.tips: The Calico Mining District was a historic silver producer. Look for dendritic agate in the volcanic tuffs on the hillsides.

digSites.name: Mojave Petrified Forest Area
digSites.summary: Remote Mojave BLM area with colorful petrified wood, agate, and jasper from ancient Miocene forests.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — BLM land. 25 lb daily limit.
digSites.tips: Look for logs partially exposed in the dry washes. The petrified wood here ranges from red to blue with stunning cell structure.

digSites.name: Bighorn Canyon Agate Beds
digSites.summary: Wyoming BLM area near Bighorn Canyon producing Montana agate, petrified wood, and jasper from the Bighorn River gravels.
digSites.tips: Walk the gravel bars along the Bighorn River. Montana agates are known for their scenic landscape-like inclusions.

digSites.name: Venice Beach Shark Teeth
digSites.summary: The 'Shark Tooth Capital of the World' — Venice Beach and Caspersen Beach yield thousands of fossilized shark teeth including megalodon.
digSites.feeInfo: Free on public beaches. Sand scoops recommended.
digSites.tips: Scoop the surf zone where waves break — black triangular shark teeth concentrate in the shell hash. Visit after storms for megalodon teeth.

digSites.name: Calvert Cliffs State Park
digSites.summary: Maryland's premier fossil collecting beach — Miocene-era shark teeth, ray plates, and whale bone fragments from the Calvert Formation.
digSites.tips: Walk the beach below the cliffs. The best teeth are found in the surf zone. DO NOT dig into the cliffs — they are unstable and protected.

digSites.name: Edinburg Geode Mine
digSites.summary: An Indiana geode mine where you can dig for geodes filled with quartz, calcite, and occasional celestite and millerite.
digSites.feeInfo: $20 per person per day. Keep all you find.
digSites.tips: Indiana geodes can contain rare millerite — hair-like metallic crystals. Crack open each geode to check for unusual mineral fills.

digSites.name: Black Cat Mountain Trilobite Quarry
digSites.summary: A commercial quarry producing world-class Devonian trilobites — enrolled phacopids, cephalons, and complete specimens.
digSites.feeInfo: $50 per person per day. Keep all fossils found.
digSites.tips: Split the dark Haragan Formation shale with a chisel — complete enrolled trilobites are common. Bring a fine brush and glue for fragile specimens.

digSites.name: Dugway Mineral Collecting Area
digSites.summary: Utah BLM area near Dugway with geodes, topaz, and red beryl in the Thomas and Dugway Ranges. Multiple collecting zones.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — BLM land. Some claims are private.
digSites.tips: Topaz in the Thomas Range fades in sunlight — wrap finds immediately. Red beryl (bixbite) is extremely rare and found only here.

digSites.name: Ray Mine Overlook Area
digSites.summary: Arizona copper mining area with azurite, malachite, and chrysocolla specimens on mine dumps. Overlook and limited collecting.
digSites.feeInfo: Free overlook. Collecting limited to designated areas.
digSites.tips: The Ray Mine is one of the largest copper mines in the world. Collect only on BLM land outside the active mine perimeter.

digSites.name: Mount Mica Mine
digSites.summary: America's oldest gem mine — discovered in 1820, Mount Mica produces world-class tourmaline, beryl, and smoky quartz.
digSites.feeInfo: Fee digs by arrangement with Coromoto Minerals. $100+ per person.
digSites.tips: Mount Mica has produced some of the finest Maine tourmaline ever found. Book well in advance — spaces are limited.

digSites.name: Strickland Quarry Park
digSites.summary: A classic Connecticut pegmatite quarry — now a town park — where collectors still find beryl, tourmaline, and columbite.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public park. Hand tools only.
digSites.tips: The old quarry dumps still produce green beryl and black tourmaline. Look in the white albite matrix near the quarry wall.

digSites.name: Bennett Quarry
digSites.summary: A famous Maine pegmatite quarry known for giant beryl crystals, tourmaline, and the world's largest morganite crystal.
digSites.feeInfo: Club access only. Contact Maine Mineralogical & Geological Society.
digSites.tips: The world's largest morganite crystal (200+ carats) came from here. Join the MMGS to access this legendary locality.

digSites.name: Rockhound Ranch
digSites.summary: A West Texas private ranch offering fee digs for agate, jasper, and fluorite in the Big Bend region.
digSites.tips: Big Bend agates are some of the most colorful in Texas. The fluorite here ranges from purple to blue and yellow.

digSites.name: Agate Creek Fossil Beds
digSites.summary: Kansas chalk badlands with mosasaur fossils, pteranodon bones, and enormous fish fossils from the Niobrara Chalk Formation.
digSites.feeInfo: Free on BLM and private land with permission.
digSites.tips: The Niobrara Chalk is rich in marine reptile fossils. Walk the gullies after rain — new fossils are exposed with each storm.

digSites.name: Pioneer Mountains Quartz Area
digSites.summary: Beaverhead-Deerlodge National Forest area near Crystal Park with smoky quartz, amethyst scepters, and clear quartz crystals.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — National Forest. $5 parking at Crystal Park.
digSites.tips: Dig in the red clay soil for quartz crystals. Scepter amethyst — a clear stem topped with a purple cap — is the prize here.

digSites.name: Santa Rosa Turquoise Mine
digSites.summary: A working Nevada turquoise mine with public collecting opportunities. Known for distinctive blue and green turquoise with spiderweb matrix.
digSites.feeInfo: $50 per person per day. Keep what you find.
digSites.tips: Nevada turquoise is prized for its spiderweb matrix patterns. Bring a small pick and brush — the turquoise is in thin veins in the host rock.

digSites.name: Wiley Well Geode Beds
digSites.summary: Popular Colorado Desert BLM area with geodes, nodules, and agate. The famous Hauser Geode Beds and Potato Patch are nearby.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — BLM land. Requires high-clearance vehicle.
digSites.tips: The Hauser Beds have the best geodes — dig in the soft volcanic ash. Coconut geodes here can contain beautiful blue and white chalcedony.

digSites.name: Dust Devil Mine
digSites.summary: A private Oregon sunstone mine offering fee digs. Find red, green, and bicolor sunstones — Oregon's state gem.
digSites.feeInfo: $75 per person per day. Keep all you find.
digSites.tips: Screen the red dirt for sunstones. The schiller effect — glittering copper flakes inside the stone — is what makes Oregon sunstone unique.

digSites.name: Payson Agate Fields
digSites.summary: Central Arizona BLM land with Payson agates — distinctive red, orange, and yellow fortification agates from the Mogollon Rim.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — BLM and National Forest land.
digSites.tips: Walk the washes and road cuts east of Payson. Payson agates are known for their warm red and orange banding.

digSites.name: Consolidated Gold Mine
digSites.summary: Historic Georgia gold mine offering underground tours and gold panning. Site of America's first gold rush in 1828.
digSites.feeInfo: Tour $18 adults, panning $8 additional. Keep any gold you find.
digSites.tips: The underground tour takes you into the original 1880s mine tunnels. Gold panning is the highlight — you keep any flakes you find.

digSites.name: Lake Erie Fossil Beach
digSites.summary: Lake Erie's north shore yields Devonian fossils — crinoid stems, brachiopods, and horn corals eroded from the Dundee Formation.
digSites.tips: Walk the beach after winter storms when fresh material washes in. Look for crinoid stem segments — small circular fossils with a star pattern.

digSites.name: Mad River Fossil Beds
digSites.summary: Ohio river beds with Ordovician fossils — bryozoans, brachiopods, and the occasional trilobite from the Cincinnati Arch.
digSites.tips: The Cincinnati Arch is world-famous for Ordovician fossils. Screen the gravel bars — the fossils are abundant and well-preserved.

digSites.name: Rocky River Sapphire Gravels
digSites.summary: North Carolina creek beds in the Spruce Pine mining district with sapphires, garnets, and rare minerals from decomposed pegmatites.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public creek access. Some areas on private land.
digSites.tips: Pan the creek gravel like gold panning. The Spruce Pine district is one of the most mineral-rich areas in the US — over 200 species found here.

digSites.name: Burnt River Gold & Agate Area
digSites.summary: Eastern Oregon BLM river area with gold panning, agate, jasper, and petrified wood. Historic Oregon gold rush country.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — BLM land. Recreational gold panning allowed.
digSites.tips: Pan the river gravel for gold — the Burnt River was a major gold producer in the 1860s. Look for agates and jasper in the same bars.

digSites.name: Cape Henlopen State Park Beach
digSites.summary: Delaware's Atlantic beaches yield fossilized shark teeth, ray dental plates, and chert pebbles from the Atlantic Coastal Plain deposits.
digSites.tips: Sift the sand and shell beds at low tide after a storm. Fossil shark teeth are dark brown to black and stand out among the white shell fragments.

digSites.name: Delaware Mineralogical Society Show
digSites.summary: Delaware's primary mineral club hosts annual shows with vendors selling minerals, fossils, gems, and lapidary materials from around the world.
digSites.feeInfo: Annual show: $5 admission. Meetings free for members.
digSites.tips: The annual spring show is the best place in Delaware to buy specimens. Join the club for field trips to nearby Pennsylvania and Maryland quarries.

digSites.name: Vernon Parish Louisiana Opal Area
digSites.summary: The only source of Louisiana Opal (a precious opal found in sandstone). Occasional public collecting on private land with permission. Rare and distinctive opal type.
digSites.feeInfo: Private land — contact local landowners for permission. Guided digs available seasonally.
digSites.tips: Louisiana Opal is extremely rare — it forms in the Catahoula Formation sandstone. The opal is found in thin seams and as matrix material. Always get landowner permission.

digSites.name: Kisatchie National Forest Petrified Wood
digSites.summary: Louisiana's national forest contains petrified wood in creek beds and stream gravels. Collecting for personal use is allowed on national forest land.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — Kisatchie National Forest. Small amounts for personal use.
digSites.tips: Search stream beds and gravel bars for petrified wood fragments. Do not collect in wilderness areas or archaeological sites. Hand tools only.

digSites.name: Voodoo Spiritual Temple & Crystal Shop
digSites.summary: New Orleans' French Quarter is home to several metaphysical and crystal shops offering tumbled stones, raw minerals, quartz clusters, and spiritual specimens.
digSites.tips: The French Quarter has multiple metaphysical shops along Decatur and Bourbon Streets. Great for unique crystal specimens and local spiritual items.

digSites.name: Mississippi Petrified Forest
digSites.summary: One of only two petrified forests in the eastern United States. Massive petrified logs from the Oligocene epoch are exposed in a ravine. Self-guided nature trails.
digSites.tips: The petrified logs here are up to 30 feet long and 15 feet around. They date from the Oligocene epoch (~36 million years ago). Great educational destination for families.

digSites.name: Vicksburg Loess Hills Fossil Area
digSites.summary: The loess bluffs along the Mississippi River contain Pleistocene-age fossils — snails, clams, and mammal bones from the last ice age.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public roadsides and some parks.
digSites.tips: Search the exposed loess (wind-blown silt) deposits along roadsides for tiny fossil snail shells. The loess formed during the Ice Age from Mississippi River floodplain dust.

digSites.name: Jackson Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Mississippi's capital has several metaphysical and crystal shops offering quartz, amethyst, local minerals, and spiritual specimens.
digSites.tips: Jackson has several metaphysical shops in the Fondren and Belhaven neighborhoods. Ask about Mississippi-derived quartz and local fossils.

digSites.name: Missouri Mines State Historic Site
digSites.summary: Former St. Joe Minerals lead mine turned museum. Massive mineral collection of galena, calcite, pyrite, and dolomite from Missouri's Lead Belt — one of the world's largest lead districts.
digSites.tips: The museum houses one of the finest mineral collections in the Midwest. The Lead Belt produced more lead than any other mining district in the world. Don't miss the giant galena cubes.

digSites.name: Elephant Rocks State Park
digSites.summary: Giant red granite boulders — some the size of elephants — stand in a line atop a granite dome. Historic granite quarry with exposed Precambrian granite formations.
digSites.tips: The elephant-shaped boulders are 1.5-billion-year-old granite. The old quarry produced granite for St. Louis buildings and pavers. Great for geology education and photography.

digSites.name: Branson Rock & Gift Shops
digSites.summary: Ozark tourist destination with multiple rock, mineral, and fossil shops. Ozark specimens include drusy quartz, galena, barite roses, and local fossils.
digSites.tips: The Branson Strip has several rock and gift shops. Look for Missouri drusy quartz — sparkling tiny crystals coating limestone or chert. Ozark barite 'desert roses' are also common.

digSites.name: Kansas City Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Kansas City's metaphysical community shops offering crystals, geodes, Missouri minerals, and spiritual specimens.
digSites.tips: Kansas City is near the Keokuk geode beds. Local shops often carry Missouri and Iowa geodes, drusy quartz, and Ozark mineral specimens.

digSites.name: Ashfall Fossil Beds State Historical Park
digSites.summary: A UNESCO-recognized fossil site where a volcanic ash fall 12 million years ago buried an entire savanna ecosystem. Rhino, horse, and camel skeletons are still being excavated.
digSites.feeInfo: Park entry $6 per vehicle. Visitor center included.
digSites.tips: One of the world's most complete Miocene fossil sites. Watch paleontologists work on skeletons in the Hubbard Rhino Barn. Great for families — kids can see real fossils being excavated.

digSites.name: Blue River Agate Area
digSites.summary: Nebraska river gravels produce distinctive agates, chert, and petrified wood washed from the Ogallala Formation. Collecting in public river access areas.
digSites.tips: Search gravel bars along the Blue and Platte Rivers. Nebraska is known for 'Nebraska Blue Agate' — a distinctive blue-gray chalcedony. Best after spring flooding.

digSites.name: Omaha Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Omaha's metaphysical community shops offering crystals, geodes, Nebraska minerals, and spiritual specimens.
digSites.tips: Omaha has a growing metaphysical scene in the Benson and Old Market districts. Look for Great Plains agates and Iowa geodes from nearby.

digSites.name: Pembina Gorge Fossil Area
digSites.summary: The Pembina Gorge exposes Cretaceous-age shale containing marine fossils — baculites, ammonites, and mosasaur fragments. Scenic badlands along the Pembina River.
digSites.tips: Search the shale outcrops along the gorge rim for baculites — straight-shelled ammonites. The Pierre Shale here is rich in late Cretaceous marine fossils.

digSites.name: Theodore Roosevelt National Park Scoria & Petrified Wood
digSites.summary: Badlands National Park with petrified wood, scoria (baked shale), and lignite coal seams. Collecting prohibited in the park, but surrounding BLM land allows it.
digSites.feeInfo: Park entry $30/vehicle (7-day pass). BLM land free.
digSites.hours: Park: daily 24 hours. Visitor center 8:00 AM – 5:00 PM.
digSites.tips: No collecting inside the national park. The surrounding BLM land south of the park has petrified wood and scoria. Scoria here is actually baked shale from burning coal seams, not volcanic.

digSites.name: Fargo Rock & Mineral Shop
digSites.summary: Fargo's mineral and fossil shop with Great Plains agates, Lake Superior agates (transported by glaciers), and specimens from the Dakota badlands.
digSites.tips: Glacial deposits brought Lake Superior agates all the way to North Dakota. Look for them in gravel pits and river gravels throughout the Red River Valley.

digSites.name: Cumberlandite Type Locality
digSites.summary: The type locality for Cumberlandite — Rhode Island's state rock. This rare titanium-rich iron ore is found in only one place in the world. Limited surface collecting.
digSites.tips: Cumberlandite is extremely dense and magnetic — it's one of the rarest rocks in the world. The outcrop is on Mineral Spring Avenue. Small hand samples can be found in the talus.

digSites.name: Newport Beach Pebble Collecting
digSites.summary: Rhode Island's Atlantic beaches yield polished beach pebbles, quartz, and occasional metamorphic minerals from glacial deposits along the rocky Narragansett Bay shoreline.
digSites.tips: The rocky Rhode Island coastline is perfect for beachcombing. Look for polished quartz, schist, and gneiss pebbles. Easton's Beach and Sachuest Beach are productive.

digSites.name: Providence Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Providence's metaphysical and crystal community shops offering quartz, amethyst, and spiritual specimens.
digSites.tips: Providence's East Side and downtown have several metaphysical shops. Ask about New England minerals — Connecticut garnet and Maine tourmaline are often available.

digSites.name: Rock of Ages Granite Quarry
digSites.summary: The world's largest deep-hole granite quarry. Tours show 550-foot-deep granite operations. Vermont's Barre Granite is world-famous for its fine grain and durability.
digSites.feeInfo: Quarry tour $18 adults, $12 children. Visitor center free.
digSites.tips: Barre Granite is over 350 million years old. The quarry is an engineering marvel — the viewing platform overlooks a massive pit. The visitor center has polished granite samples for sale.

digSites.name: Dorset Marble Quarry
digSites.summary: Historic marble quarry — the oldest operating marble quarry in the US. Vermont marble from this area was used in the Jefferson Memorial and US Supreme Court.
digSites.tips: The Norcross-West Quarry is one of the oldest in America. Vermont marble is pure white and prized for monuments. The quarry is now also a popular swimming hole.

digSites.name: Belvidere Mountain Asbestos Area
digSites.summary: Historic asbestos/serpentine mine with extensive mineral collecting. Known for serpentine, asbestos, garnet, and rare Vermont minerals. Collecting on old mine dumps.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — old mine dumps (collect at your own risk).
digSites.tips: Belvidere Mountain is Vermont's most mineral-diverse locality. Search the old mine dumps for serpentine, green garnet, and rare minerals. Avoid loose asbestos fibers — wash hands after collecting.

digSites.name: Seneca Rocks Area
digSites.summary: Dramantic Tuscarora Sandstone formations in the Spruce Knob-Seneca Rocks National Recreation Area. Road cuts and stream beds yield fossils and quartz.
digSites.tips: The Tuscarora Sandstone is 440 million years old (Silurian). Search road cuts for brachiopod fossils. The Seneca Rocks Discovery Center has geological exhibits.

digSites.name: New River Gorge Plant Fossils
digSites.summary: Carboniferous-age coal measures in the New River Gorge contain plant fossils — ferns, calamites, and seed fern impressions in shale and coal seams.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — national park. No collecting within park boundaries.
digSites.tips: No collecting inside the National River boundaries. Road cuts and stream beds outside the park have Carboniferous plant fossils in the shale overlying coal seams. Look for black fern impressions.

digSites.name: Charleston Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: West Virginia's capital has metaphysical shops offering crystals, local coal minerals, and spiritual specimens from the Appalachian region.
digSites.tips: Charleston shops often carry Appalachian quartz crystals and coal-related specimens. The WV hills produce fine quartz in vugs and veins.

digSites.name: Phoenix Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Phoenix's metaphysical community shops offering crystals, Arizona minerals, turquoise, and spiritual specimens from the desert Southwest.
digSites.tips: Phoenix has a large metaphysical scene. Look for authentic Arizona turquoise from the Bisbee and Sleeping Beauty mines. Sedona is 2 hours north for red rock specimens.

digSites.name: Denver Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Denver's metaphysical shops and the annual Denver Gem & Mineral Show — one of the largest in the US. Crystals, Colorado minerals, rhodochrosite, and aquamarine.
digSites.feeInfo: Free to browse shops. Denver Show: $15/day.
digSites.hours: Shops daily 10:00 AM – 7:00 PM. Show: September.
digSites.tips: The Denver Gem & Mineral Show in September is one of the top 3 mineral shows in the US. Year-round, shops on Broadway and South Pearl Street carry Colorado rhodochrosite and aquamarine.

digSites.name: Portland Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Portland's Hawthorne District and Alberta Arts District have numerous metaphysical shops offering crystals, Oregon sunstones, thundereggs, and spiritual specimens.
digSites.tips: Portland is a hub for Oregon specimens — sunstones from Lake County, thundereggs from central Oregon, and coastal agates. The Hawthorne District has the highest concentration of crystal shops.

digSites.name: Seattle Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Seattle's metaphysical shops in Pike Place Market and Capitol Hill offering crystals, Washington minerals, and Pacific Northwest specimens.
digSites.tips: Pike Place Market has several mineral and crystal shops. Capitol Hill has a cluster of metaphysical stores. Look for Washington quartz crystals and Oregon sunstones.

digSites.name: Austin Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Austin's metaphysical community on South Congress and East Side offering crystals, Texas topaz, and spiritual specimens.
digSites.tips: Austin's South Congress and South Lamar areas have several crystal shops. Look for Mason County topaz — Texas's state gem — which is often available in local shops.

digSites.name: Chicago Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Chicago's metaphysical shops in Andersonville and Wicker Park offering crystals, fluorite, Illinois minerals, and spiritual specimens.
digSites.tips: Chicago is the gateway to the famous Southern Illinois fluorite district. Andersonville's Clark Street has several crystal shops carrying Illinois fluorite specimens.

digSites.name: Nashville Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Nashville's metaphysical community in East Nashville and 12 South offering crystals, Tennessee minerals, and spiritual specimens.
digSites.tips: Nashville's East Side has a growing metaphysical scene. Look for Tennessee calcite, fluorite, and sphalerite from the Central Tennessee mineral district.

digSites.name: Atlanta Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Atlanta's metaphysical shops in Little Five Points and Virginia-Highland offering crystals, Georgia minerals, and spiritual specimens.
digSites.tips: Little Five Points is Atlanta's metaphysical hub. Georgia is famous for Graves Mountain rutile and lazulite — ask if local shops have Georgia specimens.

digSites.name: Santa Fe Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Santa Fe's historic plaza area metaphysical shops offering crystals, New Mexico minerals, turquoise, and spiritual specimens.
digSites.tips: Santa Fe has numerous galleries and shops on Canyon Road and the Plaza. Look for New Mexico turquoise from the Cerrillos and Tyrone mines. Authentic Native American turquoise jewelry is a specialty.

digSites.name: Asheville Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Asheville's metaphysical community — one of the largest in the Southeast. Multiple crystal shops in downtown and West Asheville offering NC minerals, gems, and spiritual specimens.
digSites.tips: Asheville is a major crystal hub. Downtown and West Asheville have many shops. Look for North Carolina sapphires, rubies, emeralds, and Hiddenite — all from the nearby Appalachian Mountains.

digSites.name: San Antonio Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: San Antonio's metaphysical shops offering crystals, Texas topaz, and spiritual specimens near the historic Pearl District and Southtown.
digSites.tips: San Antonio's Southtown and Pearl District have growing metaphysical scenes. Ask about Texas Hill Country minerals — topaz from Mason County and agates from West Texas.

digSites.name: Minneapolis Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Minneapolis metaphysical shops offering Lake Superior agates, Minnesota's state gemstone, plus crystals and spiritual specimens.
digSites.tips: Minneapolis is the gateway to Lake Superior agate country. Uptown and Northeast Minneapolis have several crystal shops. Look for the distinctive banded Lake Superior agate — Minnesota's state gem.

digSites.name: Pittsburgh Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Pittsburgh's metaphysical shops in Lawrenceville and the Strip District offering crystals, Pennsylvania minerals, and spiritual specimens.
digSites.tips: Pittsburgh is near Pennsylvania's historic mineral districts. Look for pyrite from the old coal mines and quartz from the Appalachian ridges. Lawrenceville has the most crystal shops.

digSites.name: Richmond Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Richmond's metaphysical community in Carytown and Church Hill offering crystals, Virginia minerals, and spiritual specimens.
digSites.tips: Carytown is Richmond's shopping district with several crystal shops. Virginia is famous for unakite, amazonite from Amelia County, and garnet. Ask about local Virginia minerals.

digSites.name: Salt Lake City Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Salt Lake City metaphysical shops offering crystals, Utah minerals, topaz, and spiritual specimens from the mineral-rich Wasatch region.
digSites.tips: Utah's state gem is topaz — found at Topaz Mountain in the Thomas Range. Salt Lake City shops carry Utah topaz, red beryl, and variscite. Sugar House and downtown have the most shops.

digSites.name: Las Vegas Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Las Vegas metaphysical shops offering crystals, Nevada turquoise, opal, and spiritual specimens from the mineral-rich Great Basin.
digSites.tips: Las Vegas has a surprising number of crystal shops. Look for Nevada turquoise from the Royston and Carico Lake mines. Virgin Valley opal from northern Nevada is also available.

digSites.name: Bozeman Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Bozeman's metaphysical shops offering Montana sapphires, crystals, and spiritual specimens from the mineral-rich Rocky Mountains.
digSites.tips: Bozeman is near the Rock Creek and Yogo sapphire deposits. Downtown shops carry Montana sapphires in blue, teal, and green. Ask about local Montana agates from the Yellowstone River.

digSites.name: Reno Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Reno's metaphysical shops offering crystals, Nevada minerals, turquoise, and spiritual specimens from the Great Basin region.
digSites.tips: Reno is the gateway to northern Nevada's mineral districts. Look for Virgin Valley opal, Royston turquoise, and Nevada agates. Midtown Reno has the most crystal shops.

digSites.name: Burlington Crystal & Metaphysical Shops
digSites.summary: Burlington's Church Street Marketplace area metaphysical shops offering crystals, Vermont minerals, and spiritual specimens.
digSites.tips: Burlington's Church Street has several metaphysical shops. Vermont is known for garnet, marble, and granite. Ask about local Vermont mineral specimens.

digSites.name: Calvert Cliffs State Park Fossil Beach
digSites.summary: Famous Miocene fossil site — 10-20 million year old shark teeth, whale bones, and shells erode from the cliffs. One of the East Coast's best beach fossil sites.
digSites.tips: Walk the 1.8-mile trail to the beach. Search the surf line and shell beds for dark fossil shark teeth — megalodon teeth are occasionally found here. Do NOT dig in the cliffs (dangerous and prohibited).

digSites.name: Horse Heaven Hills Agate Area
digSites.summary: Central Washington BLM desert area producing petrified wood, agate, jasper, and opalized wood. Classic Pacific Northwest desert collecting.
digSites.tips: Search dry washes and hillsides for agate and petrified wood. The area is remote — bring water and a spare tire. Spring and fall are best (too hot in summer).

digSites.name: Wausau Quartz & Pegmatite Area
digSites.summary: Central Wisconsin is known for the Nine Mile pluton — a granitic intrusion containing smoky quartz, feldspar, and rare minerals. Some quarries allow collecting.
digSites.feeInfo: Varies — some quarries charge $10–20 for collecting access.
digSites.tips: Contact local rock clubs for quarry access. The Wausau area pegmatites produce smoky quartz crystals and feldspar. The Rib Mountain area has exposed Precambrian quartzite.

digSites.name: Virginia Unakite Area
digSites.summary: The Blue Ridge Province of Virginia is the type locality for unakite — a green-and-pink granite containing epidote and feldspar. Road cuts and stream beds.
digSites.tips: Search road cuts along Route 29 and Skyline Drive area for unakite cobbles. The distinctive green-and-pink mottled stone is Virginia's signature mineral. Stream beds carry it downstream.

digSites.name: Great Salt Plains Selenite Dig
digSites.summary: The only place in the world where hourglass-shaped selenite gypsum crystals form. Digging in the salt flats produces crystals with a distinctive hourglass sand inclusion.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — state park. Crystal digging area open Apr–Oct.
digSites.tips: Dig 2 feet down in the salt flats — the hourglass selenite crystals are unique to this location. Bring a shovel, bucket, and water. The crystals have an hourglass sand inclusion visible inside the clear gypsum.

digSites.name: Columbia Fluorite District
digSites.summary: Kentucky's historic fluorspar district along the Illinois-Kentucky fluorite belt. Old mine dumps yield fluorite, calcite, barite, and sphalerite.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — old mine dumps (collect at your own risk).
digSites.tips: The KY-IL fluorite district was once the largest fluorite producer in the US. Search the old mine dumps for purple, yellow, and clear fluorite crystals. Be cautious around old mine shafts.

digSites.name: Falls of the Ohio State Park Fossil Beds
digSites.summary: 387-million-year-old Devonian fossil coral reef exposed on the Ohio River bedrock. One of the largest naturally exposed fossil beds in the US.
digSites.feeInfo: Park entry $2 per vehicle. Interpretive center $4 adults.
digSites.tips: The fossil beds are exposed when the Ohio River water level is low (late summer–fall). Walk on the ancient coral reef — corals, brachiopods, and crinoid stems are everywhere. No collecting inside the park.

digSites.name: Niobrara Chalk Fossil Beds
digSites.summary: Western Kansas exposes the Niobrara Chalk — a Cretaceous marine deposit famous for giant fish, mosasaurs, and pteranodon fossils. Monument Rocks and Castle Rock are landmarks.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — BLM and private land (get permission).
digSites.tips: Monument Rocks and Castle Rock are spectacular chalk formations. The Niobrara Chalk produces world-class Cretaceous marine fossils. Get landowner permission before collecting on private land.

digSites.name: Papakōlea Green Sand Beach
digSites.region: Ka Lae, Big Island, Hawaii, USA
digSites.summary: One of only four green sand beaches in the world. The sand is made of olivine crystals eroded from the surrounding cinder cone. Hawaii's mineral beach.
digSites.tips: The green sand is olivine — the gem variety is peridot. The 2.5-mile hike is hot and exposed — bring water. DO NOT take sand — it's protected. Appreciate the olivine crystals on the beach.

digSites.name: Jade Mountain Alaska
digSites.summary: Alaska's jade deposits in the Brooks Range. Nephrite jade boulders in stream gravels. Alaska's state gem is jade — most comes from this remote region.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — remote public land. Very difficult access.
digSites.tips: Extremely remote — accessible only by bush plane or multi-day wilderness expedition. Alaska jade is nephrite in green, white, and black varieties. Buy specimens in Anchorage shops instead.

digSites.name: Anchorage Alaska Rock & Jade Shops
digSites.summary: Anchorage rock shops specializing in Alaska nephrite jade, gold nuggets, and Alaskan minerals. The best place to buy authentic Alaska jade.
digSites.tips: Anchorage is the best place to buy authentic Alaska jade — the state gem. Look for green, white, and lavender nephrite. Gold nuggets from Alaska mining districts are also widely available.

digSites.name: Red Mountain Iron Ore Trail
digSites.summary: Birmingham was founded on iron ore from Red Mountain. The old iron ore quarries expose hematite and limonite — the minerals that built Birmingham's steel industry.
digSites.tips: Red Mountain Park covers the old iron ore mining district. The Vulcan statue overlooks the city from atop the ore formation. Look for red hematite in the trail cuts and old mine areas.

digSites.name: Palermo Mine Pegmatite
digSites.summary: Historic New Hampshire pegmatite mine famous for phosphate minerals — over 100 species including Montebrasite, purpurite, and rare lithium minerals.
digSites.feeInfo: Collecting by permission — contact local mineral clubs.
digSites.tips: Palermo is one of the world's most mineralogically diverse pegmatites. Contact the New Hampshire Mineral Club for access. Look for phosphate minerals in the altered zones around the pegmatite.

digSites.name: South Carolina Amethyst Area
digSites.summary: South Carolina's Piedmont produces amethyst in quartz veins within metamorphic rocks. The Reelfoot area and county roads yield crystals in decomposed pegmatites.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public road cuts. Private land by permission.
digSites.tips: Search decomposed pegmatite outcrops along rural roads in Abbeville County. The amethyst is typically pale to medium purple in small crystals. Join the SC Mineral and Gem Society for organized digs.

digSites.name: Black Hills Rockhound Area
digSites.summary: BLM-designated public rockhound area famous for fire agate — a brown agate that reveals an internal play of fiery red, green, and gold when carved and polished. Free collecting, no permit required.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — BLM public land. No permit required.
digSites.tips: Located on the north side of AZ Route 191, ~18 miles north of Safford, just east of milepost 141. Fire agate looks like dull brown bubbly chalcedony — carve a test window to check before carting heavy rocks home. Dispersed camping allowed up to 14 days.

digSites.name: Round Mountain Rockhound Area
digSites.region: Eastern Arizona / Western New Mexico, USA
digSites.summary: BLM-designated public rockhound area for rocks and mineral specimens. Remote desert location — bring everything you need. Managed by the Safford Field Office.
digSites.tips: From Highway 70 east of Safford, travel ~50 miles into New Mexico to just beyond milepost 5. Turn right onto the dirt access road and follow signs ~12 miles. High-clearance vehicle recommended.

digSites.name: Chambless Rock Collecting Area
digSites.summary: BLM public collecting area with hematite, magnetite, green epidote, limestone, marble, tiny dark-red garnets, and fossils in gray limestone. Multiple collecting zones along BLM Route NS328.
digSites.tips: From Needles, take I-40 west ~25 miles to Mountain Springs Rd exit. Go south on National Trails Highway west ~35 miles to BLM Route NS328 (just west of Chambless). Turn right and drive ~2 miles. Collecting area is on both sides of the route.

digSites.name: Savahia Peak Rock Collecting Area
digSites.summary: BLM public collecting area known for bright white chalcedony. Remote desert location near the Colorado River.
digSites.tips: From Needles, take US-95 south ~35 miles to BLM Route NS660 (Pyramid Peak Rd). Turn left and drive ~2 miles. Alternative: large wash north of US-62, 2 miles east of Vidal Junction — park off pavement and walk east.

digSites.name: Bete Grise Beach (Greenstone Cove)
digSites.summary: The premier chlorastrolite (Lake Superior greenstone) beach on the Keweenaw Peninsula — Michigan's state gem washes up alongside prehnite, native copper, and thomsonite on this dark cobble shoreline.
digSites.tips: Walk the cobble line after a storm. Greenstones look like plain green pebbles until wet — keep a spray bottle handy. The turtleback pattern is the tell. Beach glass and copper nuggets also turn up here.

digSites.name: Eagle Harbor Beach
digSites.summary: A productive Keweenaw beach for chlorastrolite, thomsonite, prehnite, and datolite nodules — the harbor's cobble bed catches a bit of everything the peninsula offers.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public beach and lighthouse grounds.
digSites.tips: Park at the Eagle Harbor lighthouse and walk east. The cobble line after a NW wind is most productive. Carry a small UV light — some Keweenaw datolite fluoresces.

digSites.name: Eagle River Beach
digSites.summary: Lake Superior cobble beach at the mouth of the Eagle River — agates, native copper nuggets washed from the river, and prehnite in the basalt cobbles.
digSites.tips: Walk the rivermouth bar — copper nuggets and prehnite concentrate where the river meets the lake. A metal detector helps; copper rings up unmistakably.

digSites.name: Lac La Belle Shoreline
digSites.summary: Quiet Keweenaw cobble beach at the tip of the peninsula — agates, chlorastrolite, and datolite on a less-hunted stretch of Lake Superior shore.
digSites.tips: Less crowded than Bete Grise. Walk east toward the Keweenaw Point trailhead — the cobble beds there get little pressure. Carry a spray bottle for wet-testing greenstones.

digSites.name: Keweenaw Point Cobble Beaches
digSites.summary: Remote cobble beaches at the very tip of the Keweenaw Peninsula — the least-hunted stretch on Lake Superior, with chlorastrolite, agate, datolite, and copper.
digSites.tips: Requires a hike in — no amenities. The remoteness is the draw; specimens here are often larger and less picked-over. Pack water and a daypack.

digSites.name: Delaware Mine Dump
digSites.summary: Historic Delaware Mine spoil piles — collect datolite nodules, native copper, and calcite crystals from the waste rock of one of the Keweenaw's most famous copper mines.
digSites.feeInfo: Self-guided mine tour $12–15; dump collecting included with admission.
digSites.tips: The spoil piles around the shaft collars are richest. Bring a crack hammer — datolite nodules often need to be cracked open to reveal the glassy interior. Some fluoresce under UV.

digSites.name: Central Mine Dump
digSites.summary: Public mine dumps at the ghost town of Central — native copper, datolite, and prehnite in the waste rock of the historic Central Mine.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public land. Donations to the Keweenaw County Historical Society welcome.
digSites.tips: The dumps east of the townsite are most productive. Bring a metal detector for copper and silver. Crystallized copper is the prize — look for arborescent (tree-like) growths.

digSites.name: Quincy Mine Haul Road
digSites.summary: Collect native copper and calcite crystals along the Quincy Mine haul road — one of the most accessible collecting spots in the Keweenaw.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public haul road. Quincy Mine tours $12–25 separately.
digSites.tips: Walk the haul road south of the Quincy hoist house. The rock is mine waste — copper bits and calcite crystals are common. The Quincy tours are excellent if you want underground context.

digSites.name: Mohawk #7 Mine Dump
digSites.summary: The type locality for mohawkite — collect the rare copper-arsenic mineral alongside native copper and datolite at this famous Keweenaw dump.
digSites.tips: Mohawkite is the prize — brassy-yellow metallic patches in white quartz. It's found only at this one mine on Earth. A metal detector and UV light both help; datolite nodules here can fluoresce.

digSites.name: Phoenix Mine Dump
digSites.summary: Quiet Keweenaw dump at the Phoenix townsite — native copper and prehnite in the basalt waste rock, with fewer visitors than the more famous mines.
digSites.tips: The dumps north of the old shaft are most productive. Prehnite here forms pale-green botryoidal crusts on basalt. Combine with the Keweenaw Point hike for a full day.

digSites.name: Keweenaw Bay Thomsonite Beach
digSites.summary: Thomsonite pebbles with the famous pink 'eyes' wash up on this Lake Superior cobble beach — the U.P.'s best spot for the gem-quality zeolite.
digSites.tips: Look for pebbles with concentric pink-and-white 'eyes' in the cobble line. Wet-testing is essential — the eye pattern only shows on a wet surface. Cabochon-grade thomsonite is the prize.

digSites.name: Sugarloaf Cove Agate Beach
digSites.summary: A quiet cobble cove on the Keweenaw's east shore — Lake Superior agates and thomsonite in the same beach, less picked-over than the more famous stops.
digSites.tips: Walk the cobble bar at the cove mouth after a storm. Agates glow with a waxy translucent luster when wet. Bring a spray bottle and a small trowel for turning the upper cobble layer.

digSites.name: Sand Bay Beach
digSites.summary: Sandy-gravel Keweenaw beach catching agates, chlorastrolite, and the occasional copper nugget from the surrounding basalt.
digSites.tips: Best after a southwest wind shifts the cobble line. The greenstone pebbles here are smaller than Bete Grise but more numerous — sort fast with a wet spray bottle.

digSites.name: Mohawk / Allouez Cobble Beaches
digSites.summary: Cobble beaches near the Mohawk mine district — agates, copper bits, and thomsonite wash up alongside mine-dump material.
digSites.tips: Combines beach and dump hunting in one stop. Copper bits from the nearby mines wash into the cobble line. Bring a metal detector and a UV light for the datolite.

digSites.name: Tahquamenon Falls Agate Bars
digSites.summary: River gravel bars along the Tahquamenon — agates and jasper carried downstream from Lake Superior glacial deposits.
digSites.feeInfo: Michigan state park recreation passport required ($13 annual / $7 daily).
digSites.tips: Wade the gravel bars below the Lower Falls after a spring freshet. Agates concentrate where the current slows. Combine with the nearby Whitefish Point Yooperlite beach for a full day.

digSites.name: Grand Sable Dunes Beach
digSites.summary: Wild Lake Superior beach at the base of the Grand Sable Dunes — Yooperlites, agates, and jasper on a remote stretch east of Grand Marais.
digSites.hours: Daylight hours; night UV hunting permitted.
digSites.tips: Hike in from the Log Slide overlook — about a mile to the productive cobble beds. Hunt at night with a 365nm UV light for Yooperlites; the dark basalt cobbles make the orange fluorescence pop.

digSites.name: Two Hearted River Mouth
digSites.summary: Remote rivermouth beach east of the Tahquamenon — Yooperlites and agates on a stretch made famous by Hemingway and rockhounds alike.
digSites.hours: Daylight hours; night UV hunting permitted.
digSites.tips: Drive the County Road 500 dirt road to the rivermouth. Hunt the cobble line at night with a UV light — Yooperlites are plentiful here and the beach sees few visitors.

digSites.name: Vermilion Point Beach
digSites.summary: A wild, roadless beach between Whitefish Point and Crisp Point — Yooperlites, agates, and fossil coral on the least-visited stretch of the U.P. shoreline.
digSites.hours: Daylight hours; night UV hunting permitted.
digSites.tips: Requires a hike in from the nearest forest road — pack for the day. The remoteness is the draw; specimens here are often larger and less picked-over. Bring a UV light and a spray bottle.

digSites.name: Crisp Point Beach
digSites.summary: Remote lighthouse beach west of Whitefish Point — Yooperlites, agates, and beach glass on a famously solitary stretch of Lake Superior.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — remote public land. Lighthouse donation appreciated.
digSites.hours: Daylight hours; night UV hunting permitted.
digSites.tips: The 18-mile dirt road in deters the crowds. Hunt the cobble line west of the lighthouse after a storm. Bring a UV light for night hunting — Yooperlites are abundant here.

digSites.name: Black River Harbor Cobble Beach
digSites.summary: Cobble beach at the mouth of the Black River in the western U.P. — agates, chlorastrolite, jasper, and banded iron formation jaspillite from the Porcupine Mountains.
digSites.tips: Take the Black River scenic drive to the harbor. The cobble line carries a bit of everything from the Porcupine Mountains — jaspillite (banded iron formation) is the regional specialty.

digSites.name: Porcupine Mountains Lake Superior Shore
digSites.summary: Wild Lake Superior shoreline along the Porcupine Mountains Wilderness — agates, chlorastrolite, and jaspillite banded iron formation on a remote cobble beach.
digSites.feeInfo: Michigan state park recreation passport required ($13 annual / $7 daily).
digSites.tips: Hike the Lake Superior Trail from the Union Bay trailhead. The banded iron formation (jaspillite) is the regional specialty — alternating red and silver bands, unique to this coast.

digSites.name: Union Bay Jaspillite Beach
digSites.summary: The type locality for jaspillite banded iron formation — striking alternating bands of red jasper and silver hematite on this Porcupine Mountains beach.
digSites.feeInfo: Michigan state park recreation passport required ($13 annual / $7 daily).
digSites.tips: Walk the Union Bay campground shoreline west. Jaspillite slabs litter the cobble line — the red-and-silver banding is unmistakable. Cut and polish specimens are stunning; rough is beautiful too.

digSites.name: Ontonagon River Mouth
digSites.summary: Rivermouth gravel bars at the Ontonagon — native copper nuggets and agates carried downstream from the historic Keweenaw copper district.
digSites.tips: Wade the gravel bars at the rivermouth with a metal detector — copper nuggets ring up unmistakably. Spring after ice-out is prime; fresh material washes downstream with the melt.

digSites.name: Drummond Island Dolomite Quarries
digSites.summary: Active and abandoned dolomite quarries on Drummond Island — fluorite, dolomite crystals, celestine, and sulfur-yellow calcite in the Niagara dolomite.
digSites.feeInfo: Permission required for active quarries. Some abandoned pits are accessible.
digSites.tips: Contact the Drummond Island Tourism Association for collecting access. The Niagara dolomite here is world-class for crystal specimens — celestine geodes and fluorite are the prizes.

digSites.name: Maxton Plains Alvar
digSites.summary: A rare limestone alvar plain on Drummond Island — exposed fossiliferous limestone with crinoid stems, brachiopods, and chert nodules weathering out of the bedrock.
digSites.tips: Walk the exposed limestone pavement — fossils weather out of the bedrock surface. The alvar is a rare ecosystem; tread lightly and take only loose material. Bring a small trowel.

digSites.name: Charlevoix Stone Beaches
digSites.summary: The type locality for the Charlevoix stone — fossil coral (Hexagonaria percarinata) with finer, tighter cells than the Petoskey stone, found on the Lake Michigan shoreline here.
digSites.tips: Walk the municipal beach and Michigan Beach Park after a storm. Charlevoix stones have smaller, tighter corallites than Petoskeys — wet-test with a spray bottle to make the honeycomb pattern pop.

digSites.name: Traverse City Bay Beaches
digSites.summary: The Grand Traverse Bay shoreline — Petoskey and Charlevoix stones, fossils, and chert cobbles on the public beaches of Michigan's most popular bay town.
digSites.tips: Try Clinch Park Beach and East Bay shoreline after a storm. Petoskey and Charlevoix stones both turn up — keep a spray bottle to wet-test. Spring after ice-out is prime.

digSites.name: Leland Blue Breakwater (Fishtown)
digSites.summary: Hunt for 'Leland Blue' — striking blue-green slag glass dumped into Lake Michigan by the historic Leland iron foundry — along the Fishtown breakwater and shoreline.
digSites.tips: Walk the breakwater and the rivermouth cobble line. Leland Blue is the prize — cornflower-blue slag glass that polishes like a gemstone. Petoskey and Charlevoix stones also turn up here.

digSites.name: Sleeping Bear Dunes Shoreline
digSites.summary: The Lake Michigan shoreline along Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore — Petoskey and Charlevoix stones, fossils, and beach glass on miles of wild beach.
digSites.tips: Walk the shoreline from the Dune Climb access. The wild beaches here see less pressure than Petoskey's town beach. Spring after storms is best; wet-test with a spray bottle.

digSites.name: Frankfort Beach
digSites.summary: Lake Michigan public beach at Frankfort — Petoskey and Charlevoix stones, fossils, and the occasional Lake Superior agate carried south by glacial drift.
digSites.tips: Walk the beach north of the Frankfort lighthouse after a storm. Petoskey and Charlevoix stones are common; Lake Superior agates in glacial drift are the bonus find.

digSites.name: Gulf Shores Public Beach
digSites.summary: Alabama's Gulf Coast — fossilized shell hash, Miocene fossils, and shark teeth washing out of the beach sand after storms.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public beach access. State park entry fee may apply.
digSites.tips: Sift the swash line with a fine-mesh screen after a storm. Fossil shark teeth and shell hash concentrate in the heavy-mineral layers. Dawn is best before the crowds arrive.

digSites.name: Kodiak Island Beaches
digSites.summary: Alaska's wildest rockhound beach — agates, jasper, and volcanic nodules on the cobble shores of Kodiak Island.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public beach access. Some areas require a ferry or bush plane.
digSites.tips: Access is the challenge — ferry from Homer or fly in. The beaches near the town of Kodiak are most accessible. Hunt after a storm for fresh cobble.

digSites.name: Lake Havasu Copper Canyon Cove
digSites.summary: Arizona's closest thing to a beach collecting spot — hematite-included quartz, chalcedony, and geode fragments washed down from the surrounding volcanics into a Lake Havasu cove.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public shoreline access. Lake Havasu State Park entry fee may apply.
digSites.tips: Boat or hike into the Copper Canyon cove. The cobble line carries volcanic geode fragments — crack them open for smoky quartz and chalcedony. Spring and fall are the comfortable seasons.

digSites.name: Lake Ouachita Shoreline Coves
digSites.summary: Arkansas's beach-class collecting spot — quartz crystals, novaculite fragments, and garnet schist pebbles washed from the Ouachita Mountains onto the reservoir coves.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public shoreline access. State park entry fee may apply.
digSites.tips: Hunt the coves when the lake is low — small quartz crystals and novaculite fragments concentrate on the exposed beaches. Combine with a visit to Crater of Diamonds for the full Arkansas rockhound loop.

digSites.name: San Mateo Creek Mouth / San Clemente
digSites.summary: Southern California's best beach agate spot — agate, jasper, moonstone, and occasional fossilized whale-bone fragments at the mouth of San Mateo Creek.
digSites.tips: Walk north from the San Clemente State Beach entrance to the creek mouth. Agates and jasper concentrate in the gravel after a storm. Low tide is best; check the tide tables.

digSites.name: Blue Mesa Reservoir Shoreline
digSites.summary: Colorado's beach-class collecting spot — washed pegmatite minerals (microcline, smoky quartz, garnet, tourmaline pebbles) on the reservoir beaches when water is low.
digSites.tips: Hunt the exposed beaches in late summer/fall when the reservoir is drawn down. Pegmatite minerals wash out of the surrounding granites. Bring a small trowel for turning gravel.

digSites.name: Hammonasset Beach State Park
digSites.summary: Connecticut's classic beachcombing spot — garnet-mica schist pebbles, glacial cobbles, and occasional fossil fragments on the longest public beach in the state.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — Connecticut resident; $22 non-resident weekend parking in season.
digSites.tips: Walk the swash line for garnet-mica schist pebbles — the garnets show as red specks in the schist. Glacial cobbles include a bit of everything carried south by the ice.

digSites.name: Cape Henlopen State Park Beach
digSites.summary: Delaware's barrier-island beach — fossil shark teeth, shell hash, and chert cobbles washing out of the Delaware Bay sand.
digSites.feeInfo: Delaware state park entry fee ($8 in-state / $16 out-of-state per day).
digSites.tips: Sift the swash line on the bay side (north beach) for fossil shark teeth. The bay side is calmer and concentrates heavy fossils better than the ocean side. Low tide is best.

digSites.name: Venice Beach / Caspersen Beach
digSites.summary: The 'Shark Tooth Capital of the World' — Megalodon and other fossil shark teeth wash up in the surf by the thousands on this Gulf Coast beach.
digSites.tips: Bring a 'shark tooth sifter' (a sand flea rake) and drag it through the swash line. Caspersen Beach just south of Venice is less crowded and just as productive. Megalodon teeth are the prize.

digSites.name: Tybee Island North Beach
digSites.summary: Georgia's barrier-island beach — Miocene fossils, fossilized coral, shark teeth, and chert cobbles on the north beach where the Savannah River meets the Atlantic.
digSites.tips: Walk the north beach at low tide — the rivermouth concentrates fossils. Sift the swash line for shark teeth. Spring and fall are most comfortable; summer brings crowds.

digSites.name: Punalu'u Black Sand Beach
digSites.summary: Hawaii's most famous rockhound beach — olivine and peridot grains in the basalt sand, polished basalt pebbles, and the striking black sand itself made of basalt glass.
digSites.tips: Walk the swash line for olivine grains — they're the green specks in the black sand. Take only a small sample; leave the beach as you found it. Honu (green sea turtles) bask here — give them space.

digSites.name: Bear Lake State Park Shoreline
digSites.summary: Idaho's famous 'watermelon snow' tufa nodules — pink-and-white tubular tufa formations on the Bear Lake shoreline, plus rare phosphate pebbles from the Phosphoria Formation.
digSites.feeInfo: Idaho state park entry fee ($5 per vehicle).
digSites.tips: Walk the east shore for the famous pink-and-white tufa nodules. The 'watermelon' name comes from the pink interior and white rind. Spring before the crowds is best.

digSites.name: Illinois Beach State Park / North Point Marina
digSites.summary: Lake Michigan glacial cobbles, fossiliferous Niagara dolomite pebbles, and occasional Lake Superior agates carried south by glacial drift on Illinois's only public Lake Michigan beach.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public beach access. State park parking $5.
digSites.tips: Walk the beach north toward the Wisconsin border. Lake Superior agates in glacial drift are the prize — look for the waxy translucent luster when wet. Spring after storms is best.

digSites.name: Indiana Dunes National Park Beaches
digSites.summary: Lake Superior agates in glacial drift, fossiliferous dolomite cobbles, and kyanite pebbles on the Indiana Dunes shoreline.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — national park. Parking may require a pass.
digSites.tips: Walk the Kemil Beach or Dunbar Beach access. Lake Superior agates in glacial drift are the prize — wet-test cobbles for the waxy agate luster. Spring after storms is best.

digSites.name: Coralville Lake / Lake Macbride Shoreline
digSites.summary: Devonian fossil coral — Coralville is named for it — crinoid stems, and brachiopods on the reservoir beaches after drawdowns.
digSites.tips: Hunt the exposed beaches in late summer/fall when the lake is drawn down. The Devonian fossil coral is everywhere — Coralville is literally named for it. Bring a small trowel.

digSites.name: Wilson Lake / Smoky Hill River Gravel Bars
digSites.summary: Kansas's beach-class spot — Niobrara chalk fossils, fossil shark teeth, selenite crystals, and septarian nodules in the river gravel bars and reservoir beaches.
digSites.tips: Wade the gravel bars below the Wilson Lake dam after a release. Septarian nodules (cracked mud-ball geodes) are the prize — crack them open for yellow calcite and aragonite.

digSites.name: Kentucky Lake / Land Between the Lakes Shoreline
digSites.summary: Kentucky's beach-class collecting spot — geodes, fluorite pebbles from the Illinois-Kentucky Fluorspar District, and crinoid fossils in washed limestone cobbles.
digSites.tips: Hunt the reservoir beaches when the lake is low. Fluorite pebbles (purple, yellow, blue) wash in from the famous Fluorspar District just across the Ohio River. Crinoid fossils are everywhere.

digSites.name: Grand Isle Beach
digSites.summary: Louisiana's only barrier-island beach — fossilized shell hash, chert cobbles reworked from the Citronelle Formation, and occasional fossil dolphin teeth.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public beach access. State park entry fee may apply.
digSites.tips: Sift the swash line after a storm. Fossil shell hash and chert cobbles concentrate in the heavy layers. The state park campground at the east end is a good base for a multi-day trip.

digSites.name: Pebble Beach, Islesboro
digSites.summary: Maine's famous Pebble Beach — gem-quality tourmaline, beryl, garnet, and smoky quartz pebbles weathered from surrounding pegmatites and tumbled by the sea.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public beach. Ferry from Lincolnville required.
digSites.tips: Take the state ferry from Lincolnville to Islesboro. Walk the cobble beach for tourmaline (black, watermelon) and beryl pebbles. The pegmatite pebbles here are world-famous.

digSites.name: Assateague Island Beach
digSites.summary: Maryland's barrier-island beach — fossil shark teeth, chert cobbles, and sea glass on a wild 37-mile barrier island famous for its wild horses.
digSites.feeInfo: Assateague Island National Seashore entry fee ($25 per vehicle / 7 days).
digSites.tips: Drive the oversand vehicle route (permit required) or walk north from the developed area. Shark teeth concentrate in the swash line. Watch for the wild horses — give them space.

digSites.name: Cape Cod / Nauset Beach
digSites.summary: Massachusetts's classic glacial cobble beach — garnet-mica schist pebbles, polished quartz, and occasional fossils on the outer Cape's wild ocean beach.
digSites.tips: Walk south from the Nauset Beach parking lot. Glacial cobbles include garnet-mica schist and polished quartz. The outer beach is wild and beautiful; bring a windbreaker.

digSites.name: Lutsen / Grand Marais North Shore Beaches
digSites.summary: The Minnesota North Shore's premier Lake Superior agate beaches — the state gemstone and thomsonite on the cobble beaches of Cook County.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public beach access. State park entry fee may apply.
digSites.tips: Try Lutsen Resort beach and Cutface Creek wayside. Walk the cobble line at sunrise with the sun behind you — agates glow with a waxy luster that dull rocks lack. After a storm is best.

digSites.name: Ship Island / Horn Island Beaches
digSites.summary: Mississippi's barrier-island beaches — fossil shark teeth, Miocene fossils, chert cobbles, and occasional agatized coral on the Gulf Islands National Seashore.
digSites.feeInfo: Ferry to Ship Island $30 adult / $15 child. Horn Island requires boat/kayak.
digSites.tips: Take the Ship Island ferry from Gulfport. Sift the swash line for shark teeth. Horn Island (kayak access) is wilder and less picked-over. Bring sunscreen and water — no shade.

digSites.name: Table Rock Lake Shoreline / Roark Creek Gravel Bars
digSites.summary: Missouri's beach-class collecting spot — Mozarkite (the state rock), drusy quartz, galena, and fossil crinoids in the lake-washed gravel.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public shoreline access. State park entry fee may apply.
digSites.tips: Hunt the exposed beaches and creek gravel bars when the lake is low. Mozarkite is Missouri's state rock — a colorful chert variety with swirls of pink, gray, and tan. Drusy quartz is the bonus.

digSites.name: Flathead Lake / Polson Shoreline
digSites.summary: Montana's beach-class spot — Montana moss agate, sapphire pebbles reworked from the Yogo Gulch deposit, and quartz crystals on the lake beaches.
digSites.tips: Walk the Polson shoreline and the Flathead River delta. Montana moss agate is the prize — clear chalcedony with brown/black dendritic inclusions. Yogo sapphire pebbles are the rare bonus.

digSites.name: Lake McConaughy Shoreline
digSites.summary: Nebraska's beach-class spot — Platte River agate, Blue Chalcedony, and fossilized mastodon and horse teeth eroded from the Ogallala Formation along the reservoir beaches.
digSites.feeInfo: Nebraska state park entry fee ($6 per vehicle / day).
digSites.tips: Hunt the exposed beaches when the lake is low. Platte River agate and Blue Chalcedony are the prizes. Fossil teeth erode from the Ogallala Formation bluffs — check the wave-cut bank.

digSites.name: Lake Tahoe Sand Harbor / Secret Cove
digSites.summary: Nevada's only true lake-beach rockhound spot — garnet schist pebbles, black tourmaline, quartz, and rare turquoise-stained quartz on the Tahoe east shore.
digSites.feeInfo: Nevada state park entry fee ($10 per vehicle).
digSites.tips: Walk the shoreline between Sand Harbor and Secret Cove. Garnet schist pebbles are everywhere — look for red specks in the schist. Black tourmaline (schorl) is the bonus. Summer arrives early.

digSites.name: Rye Harbor / Hampton Beach
digSites.summary: New Hampshire's coast — smoky quartz, beryl, and garnet pebbles weathered from the White Mountain granites and carried to the coast by glacial action.
digSites.feeInfo: NH state park entry fee ($4 in-state / $8 out-of-state per adult).
digSites.tips: Walk the swash line at Rye Harbor and Hampton Beach. Smoky quartz pebbles from the White Mountains are the prize — look for the brown translucent cobbles. Garnet in schist is common.

digSites.name: Cape May / Sunset Beach (Cape May Diamonds)
digSites.summary: The famous 'Cape May Diamonds' — clear quartz pebbles tumbled by the Delaware Bay — plus jasper and agate on Higbee Beach and Sunset Beach.
digSites.tips: Walk Sunset Beach at low tide — the 'Cape May Diamonds' are clear quartz pebbles that look like waterworn diamonds. Higbee Beach just west has jasper and agate in the cobble line.

digSites.name: Elephant Butte Lake Shoreline
digSites.region: Truth or Consequences, New Mexico, USA
digSites.summary: New Mexico's beach-class collecting spot — New Mexico agate, geode fragments, and turquoise-stained quartz from the surrounding Cerrillos Hills washed onto the reservoir beaches.
digSites.feeInfo: New Mexico state park entry fee ($5 per vehicle).
digSites.tips: Hunt the exposed beaches when the lake is low. New Mexico agate and geode fragments are the prizes. Turquoise-stained quartz (copper-rich) is the rare bonus from the Cerrillos Hills source.

digSites.name: Lake Erie Shoreline at Evangola State Park
digSites.summary: New York's Lake Erie beach — Devonian fossils, crinoid stems, and horn coral weathering out of the shale bluffs onto the beach.
digSites.feeInfo: NY state park entry fee ($6 per vehicle).
digSites.tips: Walk the beach at low tide and check the shale bluffs for fossils weathering out. Devonian horn coral and crinoid stems are everywhere. Spring after storms is most productive.

digSites.name: Topsail Beach (Mermaid Tears)
digSites.summary: North Carolina's barrier-island beach — semi-precious stones, fossils, and the famous 'Mermaid Tears' sea glass on the Topsail shoreline.
digSites.tips: Walk the swash line after a storm. 'Mermaid Tears' (small, well-tumbled sea glass) are the prize — Topsail is famous for them. Fossil shark teeth and semi-precious pebbles also turn up.

digSites.name: Lake Sakakawea Shoreline
digSites.summary: North Dakota's beach-class spot — petrified wood and the rare 'Teredo'-bored petrified wood from the Cannonball Formation, plus septarian nodules on the reservoir beaches.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public shoreline access. State park entry fee may apply.
digSites.tips: Hunt the exposed beaches when the lake is low. Petrified wood is the prize — the 'Teredo'-bored variety (with shipworm holes) is unique to the Cannonball Formation. Septarian nodules too.

digSites.name: Headlands Beach State Park / Mentor Headlands
digSites.summary: Ohio's Lake Erie beach — Devonian fossils (crinoid stems, horn coral, brachiopods) and occasional Lake Superior agates in glacial drift on the longest natural sand beach in Ohio.
digSites.tips: Walk the swash line and the breakwater cobble. Devonian fossils are everywhere in the shale pebbles. Lake Superior agates in glacial drift are the rare bonus — wet-test for the waxy luster.

digSites.name: Lake Murray / Lake Texoma Shoreline
digSites.summary: Oklahoma's beach-class spot — the Oklahoma 'barite rose' (the state rock) washed onto the beaches, plus selenite crystals and Permian-age fossil fragments in the lake gravel.
digSites.feeInfo: Oklahoma state park entry fee ($10 per vehicle).
digSites.tips: Hunt the exposed beaches when the lake is low. Barite roses (Oklahoma's state rock) are the prize — sand-barite crystals shaped like rose petals. Selenite crystals are common too.

digSites.name: Bandon Agate Beaches
digSites.summary: Oregon's most famous beach agate spot — agate, jasper, petrified wood, and moonstone on the southern Oregon coast at Bandon Beach and nearby Whiskey Run.
digSites.tips: Walk the swash line at low tide after a storm. Agates and jasper concentrate in the gravel. Whiskey Run Beach just south is less crowded. Winter is the best season — storms refresh the cobble.

digSites.name: Presque Isle State Park
digSites.summary: Pennsylvania's Lake Erie beach — jasper, quartz, agate, and rare Lake Superior-type agates carried to Erie by glacial drift from the Canadian Shield.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — Pennsylvania state park. Parking $5 in season.
digSites.tips: Walk the beaches on the bay side (east) for polished pebbles. Lake Superior-type agates in glacial drift are the rare prize — wet-test for the waxy luster. Spring after storms is best.

digSites.name: Block Island Beaches
digSites.summary: Rhode Island's wildest beach — glacial erratic beach pebbles, garnet schist, and polished quartz on a 17-mile island remnant of the last glaciation.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public beach access. Ferry from Point Judith required.
digSites.tips: Take the ferry from Point Judith. Walk the north end beaches (Crescent, Scotch) for glacial erratic pebbles. Block Island is a glacial moraine — the cobble is a sampler of New England geology.

digSites.name: Myrtle Beach / Pawleys Island
digSites.summary: South Carolina's barrier-island beach — phosphatic pebbles, fossil shark teeth, and Miocene fossils washing out of the beach sand.
digSites.tips: Sift the swash line at Pawleys Island (quieter than Myrtle Beach) for fossil shark teeth. Phosphatic pebbles (dark, light) are common. Spring and fall are most comfortable.

digSites.name: Lake Oahe / Oahe Dam Shoreline
digSites.summary: South Dakota's beach-class spot — the Fairburn agate (the state gemstone), prairie agates, and fossil baculites on the reservoir beaches when water is low.
digSites.tips: Hunt the exposed beaches when the lake is drawn down (late summer/fall). Fairburn agates (SD's state gem) are the prize — intricate fortification banding. Prairie agates and baculites are common too.

digSites.name: Center Hill Lake / Caney Fork Shoreline
digSites.summary: Tennessee's beach-class collecting spot — Tennessee agate, fluorite, sphalerite, and crinoid fossils in the lake-washed limestone gravel.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public shoreline access. State park entry fee may apply.
digSites.tips: Hunt the exposed beaches and creek gravel bars when the lake is low. Tennessee agate (blue-banded) is the prize. Fluorite and sphalerite from the Central Tennessee mineral district also turn up.

digSites.name: Lake Amistad Shoreline
digSites.summary: Texas's best lake-beach rockhound spot — Terlingua-type agate, fluorite, and calcite crystals washed from the surrounding West Texas volcanics onto the reservoir beaches.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public shoreline access. National recreation area entry may apply.
digSites.tips: Hunt the exposed beaches when the lake is low. Terlingua-type agate (colorful banded) is the prize. Fluorite and calcite crystals from the West Texas volcanics also wash in. Spring is best.

digSites.name: Galveston / Padre Island Beaches
digSites.summary: Texas's Gulf Coast — lightning whelk shells, fossilized shell hash, and sea glass on the long barrier-island beaches.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public beach access. State park entry fee may apply.
digSites.tips: Walk the swash line at Padre Island National Seashore (south) for the wildest hunting. Lightning whelks (the state shell) are the prize. Fossil shell hash concentrates in the heavy layers.

digSites.name: Antelope Island / Great Salt Lake Shoreline
digSites.summary: Utah's unique beach — the famous oolitic sand (tiny rounded aragonite grains unique to the Great Salt Lake), plus geode fragments and fossiliferous limestone pebbles.
digSites.feeInfo: Utah state park entry fee ($15 per vehicle).
digSites.tips: Walk the Bridger Bay shoreline for oolitic sand — tiny rounded white grains unique to this lake. Take only a small sample. Geode fragments and fossiliferous limestone pebbles are on the north shore.

digSites.name: Lake Champlain / Button Bay State Park
digSites.summary: Vermont's beach-class spot — Champlain Valley fossils (trilobites, brachiopods, the rare Isle La Motte Chazyan reefs), plus quartz and garnet pebbles on the lake beaches.
digSites.feeInfo: Vermont state park entry fee ($4 per adult).
digSites.tips: Walk the Button Bay shoreline for fossils weathering out of the shale. The Chazyan reefs at nearby Isle La Motte are some of the oldest coral reefs on Earth (450 mya). Bring a small trowel.

digSites.name: York River State Park / Fossil Beach
digSites.summary: Virginia's Miocene fossil beach — Chesapecten scallops, shark teeth, and whale bones eroding straight out of the bluff onto the beach at this York River park.
digSites.feeInfo: VA state park entry fee ($5 per vehicle).
digSites.tips: Walk the Fossil Beach trail to the York River. Chesapecten scallops (Virginia's state fossil) and shark teeth erode straight out of the bluff. Spring after storms is most productive.

digSites.name: Shi Shi Beach and Rialto Beach (Olympic Peninsula)
digSites.summary: Washington's wild Olympic coast — beach agates, jasper, fossils, polished basalt, and the famous Tree Root Fossil beds on the Shi Shi and Rialto shoreline.
digSites.feeInfo: Olympic National Park entry fee ($30 per vehicle / 7 days). Makah Reservation pass required for Shi Shi.
digSites.tips: Hike to Shi Shi Beach (3 miles) for the wildest hunting. The Tree Root Fossil beds at Rialto are striking — petrified tree roots in the wave-cut platform. Check tide tables; the beach narrows at high tide.

digSites.name: Summersville Lake Shoreline
digSites.summary: West Virginia's beach-class spot — 'coral agate' and crinoid fossils in the washed Greenbrier Limestone cobbles, plus rare quartz geodes from the New River Gorge.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public shoreline access. State park entry fee may apply.
digSites.tips: Hunt the exposed beaches when the lake is low. 'Coral agate' (silicified fossil coral) is the regional specialty. Quartz geodes from the New River Gorge also wash in. Fall drawdown is best.

digSites.name: Apostle Islands / Meyers Beach
digSites.summary: Wisconsin's Lake Superior beach — agates, thomsonite, and polished basalt and quartz pebbles from the famous sea caves of the Apostle Islands coastline.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public beach access. Apostle Islands visitor center $5.
digSites.tips: Walk the Meyers Beach cobble line and the lakeshore trail east. Lake Superior agates are the prize — wet-test for the waxy luster. Thomsonite pebbles with pink 'eyes' are the bonus.

digSites.name: Saratoga / North Platte River Gravel Bars
digSites.summary: Wyoming's beach-class collecting spot — Wyoming jade (nephrite) pebbles, plus rare Wyoming iolite and diamond fragments from the State Line district, in the river gravels.
digSites.tips: Wade the gravel bars below Saratoga after a spring freshet. Wyoming jade (nephrite) pebbles are the prize — olive-green, tough, and waxy. The river gravels also carry iolite and rare diamond fragments.

digSites.name: Yonaguni / Irabu Shell-Sand Beaches
digSites.summary: The famous tiny-sea-shell beaches of Okinawa — the sand itself is almost entirely made of countless tiny foraminifera and micro-gastropod shells, a globally unique beach class.
digSites.tips: Look closely at the 'sand' — it's almost entirely tiny shells. Bring a hand lens or jeweler's loupe to see the foraminifera and micro-gastropods. Take only a small sample. Snorkel the reef too.

digSites.name: Okinawa Main-Island Shell Beaches
digSites.summary: The broader Okinawa shell-sand beaches — star sand (foraminifera), coral fragments, and micro-gastropods on the islands of the Ryukyu archipelago.
digSites.tips: Ishigaki and Miyako islands have the most famous 'star sand' beaches. The 'stars' are foraminifera tests — look closely with a hand lens. Local shops sell polished star-sand vials.

digSites.name: Hokkaido / Toyama Bay Beach Jade
digSites.summary: Famous beach jade (nephrite) cobbles on the Sea of Japan coast — the Itoigawa 'Jade Gorge' deposits wash nephrite cobbles onto the Niigata and Toyama bay beaches.
digSites.tips: Itoigawa is the type locality for Japanese jade — the Kotogahama beach is most famous. Nephrite cobbles look like tough, waxy green-gray rocks; tap-test with a hammer for the jade ring.

digSites.name: Jurassic Coast — Lyme Regis & Charmouth
digSites.summary: One of the most famous fossil-collecting beaches in the world — ammonites, belemnites, ichthyosaur and plesiosaur vertebrae, crinoids, and the famous Lyme Regis pyritized ammonites weather out of the cliffs.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public beach. Collecting code: pick only loose material from the foreshore; never hammer the cliffs.
digSites.tips: Visit after a winter storm when fresh material falls from the cliffs. Never dig into the cliff itself; collect only loose fossils from the foreshore. The Lyme Regis Museum runs guided fossil walks.

digSites.name: Lulworth Cove & Kimmeridge Bay
digSites.summary: The famous 'Fossil Forest' ledges and oil shale of Kimmeridge Bay, plus the iconic folded limestone of Lulworth Cove — ammonites and fossil wood in the Kimmeridge Clay.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public beach. Lulworth Estate parking £5–8.
digSites.tips: Walk east from Kimmeridge Bay to see the Fossil Forest ledges (preserved Jurassic tree stumps). Ammonites weather out of the Kimmeridge Clay — check the foreshore slabs. Check tide tables.

digSites.name: Cornwall Beach Pebbles & Stream Gravels
digSites.summary: Cornish beach pebbles and stream gravels — cassiterite (tin oxide) in the stream gravels, plus the famous Cornish 'puddingstone'-style pebbles on the beach.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public beach and stream access.
digSites.tips: Pan the stream gravels near St. Just for cassiterite (the historic Cornish tin ore). The beach pebbles include the famous Cornish puddingstone. Combine with a visit to the Geevor Tin Mine.

digSites.name: Cape York Beach Agates & Boulder Opal
digSites.summary: Cape York's wild Gulf beaches — beach agates, fossilized wood, and boulder opal fragments washing out of the Cretaceous sediments along the remote northern coast.
digSites.feeInfo: Free — public beach access. Remote; 4WD required.
digSites.tips: Remote — drive the Cape York Development Road in the dry season (May–Oct). Beach agates and boulder opal fragments wash out of the ironstone bluffs. Carry water and a satellite communicator.

digSites.name: Birmingham Rock & Mineral Shop
digSites.summary: Birmingham's long-standing rock and mineral shop carrying Alabama hematite, local fossils, and a wide selection of cabochons and tumbling rough.
digSites.tips: Ask about the Alabama hematite specimens — Red Mountain ore samples are a regional specialty. The owner keeps uncut local rough in the back.

digSites.name: Huntsville Crystal Corner
digSites.summary: A metaphysical crystal shop in Huntsville carrying quartz clusters, amethyst geodes, selenite, and a curated selection of tumbled stones.
digSites.tips: Good source for Alabama-grown quartz from the Piedmont. Metaphysical focus but the specimen quality is real — check the geode room.

digSites.name: Gulf Coast Fossil & Mineral
digSites.summary: Mobile shop specializing in Gulf Coast Miocene fossils — megalodon teeth, whale ear bones, and shell fossils — plus Southeastern minerals.
digSites.tips: Best Gulf Coast fossil selection in Alabama. Megalodon teeth from the local rivers are the specialty — ask for the runner-up bucket for affordable smaller teeth.

digSites.name: Alaska Jade & Gift
digSites.summary: Fairbanks shop specializing in authentic Alaska nephrite jade from the Brooks Range — the state gem — plus gold nuggets and Alaskan minerals.
digSites.hours: Daily 9:00 AM – 9:00 PM (summer); Mon–Sat 10:00 AM – 6:00 PM (winter)
digSites.tips: The real deal for Alaska jade — green, white, and lavender nephrite, all from the Kobuk valley. Gold nuggets by the gram are a popular souvenir.

digSites.name: Anchorage Rock Shop
digSites.summary: Anchorage's full-service rock shop with Alaska jade, gold nuggets, soapstone, and a wide lapidary supply section for the local carving community.
digSites.tips: The lapidary supply corner is the real draw if you carve — Alaska jade rough, soapstone blocks, and carving tools. Gold nugget pendants are a tourist favorite.

digSites.name: Juneau Crystal Corner
digSites.summary: Juneau metaphysical crystal shop carrying quartz, amethyst, and a curated selection of tumbled stones — a cozy stop in Southeast Alaska.
digSites.tips: Small but well-curated. The owner sources quartz from local Southeast Alaska prospects. Hours are seasonal — call ahead in winter.

digSites.name: Meteor Crater Gift Shop
digSites.summary: The Meteor Crater visitor center gift shop — Canyon Diablo meteorite fragments, tektites, and a strong selection of Southwestern minerals.
digSites.feeInfo: Free to browse with crater admission ($18 adult).
digSites.tips: Meteorite fragments are the draw — Canyon Diablo iron meteorite pieces from the crater itself. Certificate of authenticity included. Great Arizona minerals too.

digSites.name: Four Peaks Mining & Mineral
digSites.summary: Scottsdale shop specializing in Arizona's famous copper minerals — turquoise, malachite, azurite, chrysocolla — plus Four Peaks amethyst from the local mine.
